knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variational Inequality Associated with a Convex Function and a Maximally Monotone Operator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a Hilbert-space variational inequality generated by a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function and a set-valued maximally monotone operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a Hilbert space, let \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), and let \(B:\mathcal H\to2^{\mathcal H}\) be maximally monotone. The associated variational inequality is to find \(x\in\mathcal H\) such that \((\exists u\in Bx)(\forall y\in\mathcal H)\;\langle x-y,u\rangle+f(x)\leq f(y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function f and a maximally monotone operator B on a Hilbert space, find x and some u in Bx such that the inner product of x−y with u plus f(x) is at most f(y) for every y in the space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Sol}=\{x\in\mathcal H\mid(\exists u\in Bx)(\forall y\in\mathcal H),\ \langle x-y,u\rangle+f(x)\leq f(y)\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A point \(x^*\in C\) solves the Stampacchia variational inequality for \(F\) on \(C\) precisely when
\[\langle F(x^*),y-x^*\rangle\ge 0\qquad\text{for every }y\in C.\]
The set of all such points is denoted by \(\operatorname{SOL}_S(F,C)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Stampacchia solution evaluates the operator at the candidate point and has nonnegative pairing with every feasible displacement.
knowledge_statements.title: Stampacchia Variational Inequality

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A point \(x^*\in C\) solves the Minty variational inequality for \(F\) on \(C\) precisely when
\[\langle F(y),y-x^*\rangle\ge 0\qquad\text{for every }y\in C.\]
Thus the operator is evaluated at each comparison point \(y\), rather than at \(x^*\). The solution set is denoted by \(\operatorname{SOL}_M(F,C)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Minty solution pairs the operator at every comparison point with its displacement from the candidate and requires all pairings to be nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.title: Minty Variational Inequality

knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Correspondence Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotone, segment-hemicontinuous Hilbert-space correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(C\subseteq H\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(F:C\to H\). Assume that \(\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle\ge 0\) for every \(x,y\in C\), and that for every \(x,y\in C\) the map \(t\mapsto\langle F(x+t(y-x)),y-x\rangle\), defined for \(t\in[0,1]\), is right-continuous at \(t=0\). Then, for every \(x^*\in C\),
\[x^*\in\operatorname{SOL}_S(F,C)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x^*\in\operatorname{SOL}_M(F,C).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a monotone operator that is right-continuous along feasible segments, the Stampacchia and Minty solution sets coincide.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(C\subseteq H\) is nonempty and convex.
\(F:C\to H\) is monotone and right-continuous at the initial point of every segment in \(C\) in the stated scalar-pairing sense.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{SOL}_S(F,C)=\operatorname{SOL}_M(F,C)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Pseudomonotone Correspondence Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise pseudomonotonicity with segment hemicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(C\subseteq H\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(F:C\to H\). Assume that, for every \(x,y\in C\),
\[\langle F(x),y-x\rangle\ge0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\langle F(y),y-x\rangle\ge0,\]
and that the map \(t\mapsto\langle F(x+t(y-x)),y-x\rangle\), defined for \(t\in[0,1]\), is right-continuous at \(t=0\). Then, for every \(x^*\in C\),
\[x^*\in\operatorname{SOL}_S(F,C)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x^*\in\operatorname{SOL}_M(F,C).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a pointwise pseudomonotone operator that is right-continuous along feasible segments, the Stampacchia and Minty solution sets coincide.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(C\subseteq H\) is nonempty and convex.
\(F:C\to H\) satisfies the displayed pointwise pseudomonotonicity implication and segment right-continuity condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{SOL}_S(F,C)=\operatorname{SOL}_M(F,C)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(C=[0,1]\) and \(F(x)=1-2x\), direct evaluation of
\[F(x^*)(y-x^*)\ge0\qquad(y\in C)\]
gives \(\operatorname{SOL}_S(F,C)=\{0,\tfrac12,1\}\). In contrast, the Minty inequalities \(F(y)(y-x^*)\ge0\) force \(x^*\le0\) from \(y<\tfrac12\) and \(x^*\ge1\) from \(y>\tfrac12\), with incompatible endpoint inequalities; thus \(\operatorname{SOL}_M(F,C)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decreasing affine operator on an interval has three Stampacchia solutions but no Minty solution, showing that nonmonotonicity can separate the concepts.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonmonotone Solution-Concept Separation

source_refs.locator: I.2 The Characterization of the Projection onto a Convex Set p. 8
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(N_C(x)=\{v\in H:\langle v,y-x\rangle\le0\text{ for every }y\in C\}\) for \(x\in C\). Then \(x^*\in C\) solves the Stampacchia VI exactly when
\[0\in F(x^*)+N_C(x^*).\]
Because \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, this is also equivalent, for every \(\lambda>0\), to
\[x^*=P_C\bigl(x^*-\lambda F(x^*)\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a closed convex set, a VI is equivalently a normal-cone inclusion or a fixed point of a projected operator step.
knowledge_statements.title: Closed Convex-Set VIs

children.title: Polyhedral Feasible-Set VIs
children.top_down_role: VI structure associated with general polyhedral feasible sets.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\) solves the VI exactly when it admits multipliers satisfying the displayed linear complementarity conditions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplier representation for inequality-defined polyhedra.

source_refs.locator: 2.4.3 Polyhedrality of the solution set p. 180
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A point \(x^*\in C\) solves the Stampacchia VI if and only if there exists \(\lambda^*\in\mathbb R^m\) such that
\[F(x^*)+A^{\mathsf T}\lambda^*=0,\qquad \lambda^*\ge0,\qquad Ax^*\le b,\qquad \lambda^*\odot(Ax^*-b)=0.\]
Thus a VI over a polyhedron has a finite multiplier and complementarity representation, including redundant inequality descriptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A VI on an inequality-defined polyhedron is equivalent to stationarity, primal feasibility, nonnegative multipliers, and complementary slackness.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Feasible-Set VIs

knowledge_statements.title: Box-Constrained VIs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite box with coordinatewise characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n\in\mathbb N\), let \(C=\prod_{i=1}^n[\ell_i,u_i]\subset\mathbb R^n\), where \(-\infty<\ell_i<u_i<\infty\), and let \(F:C\to\mathbb R^n\). A point \(x^*\in C\) solves the Stampacchia variational inequality if and only if, for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\),
\[\begin{cases}F_i(x^*)\ge0,&x_i^*=\ell_i,\\F_i(x^*)=0,&\ell_i<x_i^*<u_i,\\F_i(x^*)\le0,&x_i^*=u_i.\end{cases}\]
These conditions are equivalent to \(0\in F(x^*)+N_C(x^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a finite box, each operator component is nonnegative at its lower bound, zero in the coordinate interior, and nonpositive at its upper bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\) solves the VI exactly when every coordinate satisfies the displayed bound-dependent sign condition.

notation.meaning: The ith component of the operator
Lower and upper bounds for coordinate i
Convex normal cone to the box

source_refs.locator: 9.4.3 Box constrained VIs p. 869
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The box has the polyhedral representation
\[C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:x_i\le u_i,
\ -x_i\le-\ell_i\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,n\}.\]
For \(x\in C\), its normal cone is
\[N_C(x)=\operatorname{cone}\bigl(\{e_i:x_i=u_i\}\cup\{-e_i:x_i=\ell_i\}\bigr).\]
Consequently, box-constrained VIs are polyhedral VIs whose active constraint normals are signed coordinate vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite box is a bounded polyhedron, and its normal cone is generated by signed coordinate vectors at active bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Box Geometry as a Polyhedral Specialization

Given \(\ell,u\in\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(\ell\le u\) componentwise, define
\[
\operatorname{Box}[\ell,u]=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\ell\le x\le u\},
\]

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cone VI is equivalent to \(x^*\in K\), \(F(x^*)\in K^*\), and \(\langle F(x^*),x^*\rangle=0\).

source_refs.locator: I.4 Variational Inequalities p. 13
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K^*=\{z\in H:\langle z,y\rangle\ge0\text{ for every }y\in K\}\). A point \(x^*\in K\) satisfies
\[\langle F(x^*),y-x^*\rangle\ge0\qquad\text{for every }y\in K\]
if and only if
\[F(x^*)\in K^*,\qquad \langle F(x^*),x^*\rangle=0.\]
Hence a VI over a cone is precisely a cone complementarity problem under the positive-dual convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone-constrained VI is equivalent to primal cone membership, dual cone membership of the operator value, and orthogonality between them.
knowledge_statements.title: Cone-Constrained VIs

knowledge_statements.title: Cartesian-Product VIs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite Cartesian products of real Hilbert spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m\in\mathbb N\), let \(H_i\) be a real Hilbert space, and let \(C_i\subseteq H_i\) be nonempty for each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\). Equip \(H=H_1\times\cdots\times H_m\) with its canonical product inner product, set \(C=C_1\times\cdots\times C_m\), and let \(F=(F_1,\ldots,F_m):C\to H\). For \(x^*=(x_1^*,\ldots,x_m^*)\in C\),
\[\sum_{i=1}^m\langle F_i(x^*),y_i-x_i^*\rangle_{H_i}\ge0\qquad\text{for every }y=(y_1,\ldots,y_m)\in C\]
holds if and only if, for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\),
\[\langle F_i(x^*),z_i-x_i^*\rangle_{H_i}\ge0\qquad\text{for every }z_i\in C_i.\]
Each \(F_i(x^*)\) may depend on the full vector \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variational inequality on a finite Cartesian product of Hilbert spaces is equivalent to one inequality per block, while each block operator may depend on all blocks.
assumptions_latex: \(m\in\mathbb N\), each \(H_i\) is a real Hilbert space, and each \(C_i\subseteq H_i\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The product-space VI holds exactly when every displayed component VI holds.

children.title: Monotone Operators
children.top_down_role: The baseline monotonicity regime for VI operators.

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty subset of a real Hilbert space \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is monotone on \(C\) exactly when the displayed two-point inequality holds for every pair in \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-valued Hilbert-space monotonicity.

source_refs.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The operator \(F\) is monotone on \(C\) when
\[\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle\ge0\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in C.\]
This definition permits equality for distinct points; strict monotonicity instead requires a strict inequality whenever \(x\ne y\). No continuity, convexity of \(C\), or maximality is included in monotonicity itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An operator is monotone when differences of its values have nonnegative inner product with the corresponding differences of points.
knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle>0\) whenever \(x,y\in C\) and \(x\ne y\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The operator \(F\) is strictly monotone on \(C\) if
\[\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle>0\qquad\text{for every distinct }x,y\in C.\]
Thus strict monotonicity strengthens monotonicity by requiring strict positivity for every nonzero displacement between domain points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An operator is strictly monotone when its value difference has strictly positive inner product with every nonzero difference of domain points.
knowledge_statements.title: Strictly Monotone Operators

children.title: Strictness Boundary for Monotonicity
children.top_down_role: Distinctions that separate strict monotonicity from ordinary monotonicity.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Monotonicity does not imply strict monotonicity.

notation.meaning: a fixed vector in the Hilbert space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete boundary separating ordinary from strict monotonicity.

source_refs.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For any fixed \(c\in H\), define \(F:C\to H\) by \(F(x)=c\). Then
\[\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle=0\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in C.\]
Hence \(F\) is monotone, but it is not strictly monotone because equality persists for every pair of distinct points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant operator is monotone because every monotonicity pairing is zero, but it is never strictly monotone on a domain containing distinct points.
knowledge_statements.title: Strictness Boundary for Monotonicity

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle\ge \mu\|x-y\|^2\) for all \(x,y\in C\), for some \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard Hilbert-space strong-monotonicity convention.

source_refs.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The operator \(F\) is strongly monotone on \(C\) with modulus \(\mu>0\) if
\[\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle\geq \mu\|x-y\|^2\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in C.\]
This inequality implies strict monotonicity whenever \(x\ne y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong monotonicity lower-bounds the monotonicity pairing by a positive multiple of the squared distance between the two points.
knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Monotone Operators

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty subset of a real Hilbert space \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle\ge \beta\|F(x)-F(y)\|^2\) for all \(x,y\in C\), for some \(\beta>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard inverse-strong-monotonicity convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The operator \(F\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive on \(C\), for \(\beta>0\), if
\[\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle\geq \beta\|F(x)-F(y)\|^2\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in C.\]
In particular, every cocoercive operator is monotone and is \(1/\beta\)-Lipschitz on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cocoercivity controls the squared change in operator values by their monotonicity pairing; it implies both monotonicity and Lipschitz continuity.
knowledge_statements.title: Cocoercive Operators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula and its monotonicity and Lipschitz consequences are standard, but the record supplies no citation or inspectable locator. An authoritative source is required before the candidate can be accepted.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of cocoercivity through averagedness of the associated forward mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathcal H\) be nonempty, let \(T:D\to\mathcal H\), let \(\beta>0\), and let \(\gamma\in(0,2\beta)\). Then \[T\text{ is }\beta\text{-cocoercive}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \operatorname{Id}-\gamma T\text{ is }\frac{\gamma}{2\beta}\text{-averaged}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For beta positive and gamma strictly between zero and 2 beta, T is beta-cocoercive exactly when the forward mapping identity minus gamma T is gamma/(2 beta)-averaged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\text{ is }\beta\text{-cocoercive}\iff \operatorname{Id}-\gamma T\text{ is }\frac{\gamma}{2\beta}\text{-averaged}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The pair \((C,F)\) satisfies the \(\rho\)-weak Minty condition if there exists \(x^\star\in C\) such that
\[\langle F(x),x-x^\star\rangle\geq-\frac{\rho}{2}\|F(x)\|^2\qquad\text{for every }x\in C.\]
At \(\rho=0\), this reduces to the usual Minty inequality with reference point \(x^\star\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is integrable precisely when \(F=\nabla\phi\) on \(U\) for some \(\phi\in C^1(U)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional potential representation of a VI operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The VI operator \(F\) is integrable, or a potential operator, on \(U\) if there exists a continuously differentiable function \(\phi:U\to\mathbb R\) satisfying
\[F(x)=\nabla\phi(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in U.\]
The function \(\phi\) is determined up to an additive constant on each connected component of \(U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integrable VI operator is exactly the gradient of a continuously differentiable scalar potential on its domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Integrable VI Operators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The gradient-potential formulation is mathematically standard and the definition content kind fits the leaf, but the record has no source or inspectable locator. An authoritative source should confirm the intended meaning of integrability in this VI taxonomy.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is no \(\phi\in C^2(\mathbb R^2)\) satisfying \(F=\nabla\phi\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rotation field as a canonical smooth nonpotential operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(F(x_1,x_2)=(-x_2,x_1)\), the Jacobian is
\[DF(x)=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\]
which is not symmetric. If \(F=\nabla\phi\) for some \(\phi\in C^2(\mathbb R^2)\), then \(DF=\nabla^2\phi\) would be symmetric. Therefore this smooth VI operator admits no twice continuously differentiable scalar potential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The planar rotation field is nonpotential: its nonsymmetric Jacobian cannot be the Hessian of a twice continuously differentiable scalar function.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonpotential VI Operators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rotation field is a standard smooth nonpotential example, but no source or locator is supplied. The statement also contains proof text, and its formal conclusion excludes only a \(C^2\) potential while the plain text asserts nonpotentiality without stating the regularity bridge to the earlier \(C^1\)-potential definition. Source-backed revision is required.

\[

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The affine field \(F(x)=Mx+q\) is monotone on \(C\) when
\[
\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle\ge0
\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in C.
\]
Equivalently, it is monotone on \(C\) if and only if
\[
\langle Mz,z\rangle\ge0
\qquad\text{for every }z\in C-C.
\]
If monotonicity is required on all of \(\mathbb{R}^n\), this holds if and only if the symmetric part \(\tfrac12(M+M^\mathsf{T})\) is positive semidefinite, equivalently \(M+M^\mathsf{T}\succeq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine field is monotone on the feasible set when its quadratic form is nonnegative on every feasible difference. Global monotonicity is equivalent to positive semidefiniteness of the symmetric part of its linear term, and the constant term has no effect.
knowledge_statements.title: Monotone AVIs

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the transformed-point convention, an implicit variational inequality seeks \(x^\star\in X\) such that \(g(x^\star)\in C\) and
\[
\langle F(x^\star),y-g(x^\star)\rangle_H\ge0
\qquad\text{for every }y\in C.
\]
Equivalently, with the Hilbert-space normal cone to \(C\), the defining inclusion is
\[
0\in F(x^\star)+N_C(g(x^\star)).
\]
The ordinary VI is recovered when \(X=H\) and \(g\) is the identity mapping.

\[
\text{find }x^\star\in C\text{ such that }f(x^\star,y)\ge0

\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in C.

dot\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in C,
\]
implies this pseudomonotonicity condition.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact correspondence for the bifunction induced by a single-valued Hilbert-space operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the bifunction induced by \(F\) as
\[
f_F(x,y)=\langle F(x),y-x\rangle_H
\qquad\text{for }x,y\in C.
\]
Then \(f_F(x,x)=0\), and for every \(x^\star\in C\),
\[
\langle F(x^\star),y-x^\star\rangle_H\ge0\text{ for every }y\in C
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
f_F(x^\star,y)\ge0\text{ for every }y\in C.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{VI}(F,C)=\operatorname{EP}(f_F,C).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every single-valued VI is exactly an equilibrium problem for the bifunction formed by pairing the operator with feasible displacements.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Hilbert-space variational inequality determined by \(F\) and \(C\) is to find \(x^\star\in C\) such that
\[
\langle F(x^\star),y-x^\star\rangle_H\ge0
\qquad\text{for every }y\in C.
\]
For the normal cone
\[
N_C(x)=\{v\in H:\langle v,y-x\rangle_H\le0\text{ for every }y\in C\},
\]
the VI is equivalent to the inclusion
\[
0\in F(x^\star)+N_C(x^\star).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hilbert-space VI seeks a feasible point where the operator pairs nonnegatively with every feasible displacement.
knowledge_statements.title: Hilbert-Space VIs

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a real Banach space, let \(C\subset X\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(F:C\to X^*\). The Banach-space variational inequality \(\operatorname{VI}(C,F)\) asks for \(\bar x\in C\) such that
\[
\langle F(\bar x),y-\bar x\rangle_{X^*,X}\ge 0\qquad\text{for every }y\in C.
\]
Here the inequality is scalar and uses the canonical duality pairing. Closedness of \(C\), continuity or monotonicity of \(F\), and geometric properties of \(X\) are additional hypotheses used for existence or algorithmic results, not part of the problem definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Banach-space VI seeks a feasible point whose operator value has nonnegative dual pairing with every feasible displacement.
knowledge_statements.title: Banach-Space VIs

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed symmetric positive-definite metric in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the \(H\)-metric projection by \(P_C^H(u)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in C}\tfrac12\|y-u\|_H^2\). For every \(x\in C\) and \(\alpha>0\),
\[
x\in\operatorname{SOL}(C,F)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x=P_C^H\bigl(x-\alpha H^{-1}F(x)\bigr).
\]
The weighted projection condition is \(\langle H(x-u),y-x\rangle\ge0\) for every \(y\in C\). Substitution of \(u=x-\alpha H^{-1}F(x)\) reduces it to \(\langle F(x),y-x\rangle\ge0\) for every \(y\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The VI is equivalently a fixed-point equation for projection in any fixed positive-definite metric, with the operator step scaled by the inverse metric.
knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Metric Projection Representation

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(T:C\to C\) by \(T(x)=P_C(x-\alpha F(x))\) and set \(q=\sqrt{1-2\alpha\mu+\alpha^2L^2}\). Then \(0\le q<1\) and
\[
\|T(x)-T(y)\|\le q\|x-y\|\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in C.
\]
The map \(T\) has a unique fixed point \(x^*\in C\), which is the unique solution of \(\operatorname{VI}(C,F)\). Moreover, for every \(x^0\in C\), the iteration \(x^{k+1}=T(x^k)\) satisfies
\[
\|x^k-x^*\|\le q^k\|x^0-x^*\|.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the strongly monotone and Lipschitz Euclidean regime, a suitable projected forward step is contractive, has the unique VI solution as its fixed point, and converges globally at a linear rate bounded by its contraction factor.
knowledge_statements.title: Contractive Fixed-Point Regime

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Averaged-operator regime without a strict contraction assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(F\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive, meaning
\[
\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle\ge\beta\|F(x)-F(y)\|^2
\]
for all \(x,y\in C\). For \(0<\alpha<2\beta\), the forward map \(I-\alpha F\) is averaged, and its composition with the firmly nonexpansive projection \(P_C\) is averaged. Hence \(T=P_C\circ(I-\alpha F)\) is nonexpansive but need not have Lipschitz modulus strictly below one. Nevertheless,
\[
\operatorname{Fix}T=\operatorname{SOL}(C,F).
\]
Thus fixed-point algorithms based on averagedness apply even when Banach contraction theory does not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cocoercivity makes the projected forward map averaged and nonexpansive; its fixed points remain exactly the VI solutions even without strict contraction.
knowledge_statements.title: Noncontractive Fixed-Point Representations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The averaged-operator conclusion is plausible and standard, but no source is supplied. knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(N_C(x)=\{v\in H:\langle v,y-x\rangle\le0\text{ for every }y\in C\}\) for \(x\in C\), and \(N_C(x)=\varnothing\) otherwise. Then
\[
x\in\operatorname{SOL}(C,F)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
-F(x)\in N_C(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
0\in F(x)+N_C(x).
\]
Thus the feasible-set constraint and all VI test inequalities are encoded by the normal-cone operator. The equivalence is algebraic and does not require monotonicity of \(F\); monotonicity becomes relevant to the properties and solution methods of the resulting inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The VI is exactly the zero-inclusion problem obtained by adding the feasible set's normal cone to the original operator.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Cone Inclusion Reformulation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward-resolvent representation of a two-operator inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\gamma>0\), define the resolvent \(J_{\gamma A}=(I+\gamma A)^{-1}\). Then
\[
0\in A(x)+B(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x=J_{\gamma A}\bigl(x-\gamma B(x)\bigr).
\]
A constrained VI is recovered by taking \(A=N_C\) and \(B=F\), in which case \(J_{\gamma N_C}=P_C\). More generally, choosing \(A=\partial g+N_C\) separates nonsmooth and constraint structure from the explicit field \(B\). The equivalence itself requires only the resolvent definition; additional cocoercivity or Lipschitz assumptions govern convergence of forward-backward iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Splitting the VI operator into implicit and explicit parts turns its zero inclusion into a resolvent fixed-point equation suitable for operator splitting.
knowledge_statements.title: Structured Operator-Sum Reformulation

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\alpha>0\), define the natural map on \(\mathbb R^n\) by
\[
R_\alpha(x)=x-P_C\bigl(x-\alpha F(x)\bigr).
\]
Then
\[
R_\alpha(x)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x=P_C\bigl(x-\alpha F(x)\bigr)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x\in\operatorname{SOL}(C,F).
\]
In particular, any zero is automatically feasible because it equals a point in the range of \(P_C\). Thus the constrained variational inequality is represented by the unconstrained nonsmooth equation \(R_\alpha(x)=0\), and \(\|R_\alpha(x)\|\) is a residual vanishing exactly at solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtracting the projected forward step from the current point gives a natural residual whose zeros coincide exactly with VI solutions.
knowledge_statements.title: Natural-Map Equation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unscaled Euclidean normal map for a polyhedral feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the normal map
\[
F_C(z)=F(P_Cz)+z-P_Cz,
\qquad z\in\mathbb R^n.
\]
If \(F_C(z)=0\) and \(x=P_Cz\), then \(z-x=-F(x)\in N_C(x)\), so \(x\in\operatorname{SOL}(C,F)\). Conversely, if \(x\) solves the VI, then \(z=x-F(x)\) satisfies \(P_Cz=x\) and \(F_C(z)=0\). For polyhedral \(C\), the projection \(P_C\) is piecewise affine on a finite polyhedral subdivision. Consequently, when \(F\) is affine, the normal map \(F_C\) is piecewise affine.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polyhedral normal map converts the VI into an equation; affine fields yield a piecewise-affine equation because projection onto a polyhedron is piecewise affine.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Normal Maps

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a parameter \(\rho>0\), define
\[
F_{C,\rho}(z)=F(P_Cz)+\rho^{-1}(z-P_Cz).
\]
If \(F_{C,\rho}(z)=0\) and \(x=P_Cz\), then \(z-x=-\rho F(x)\in N_C(x)\), because the normal cone is positively homogeneous; hence \(x\) solves \(\operatorname{VI}(C,F)\). Conversely, if \(x\) solves the VI, then \(z=x-\rho F(x)\) satisfies \(P_Cz=x\) and \(F_{C,\rho}(z)=0\). Thus every positive scaling preserves the solution correspondence while changing the equation's scaling and potentially its numerical conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive scaling of the normal correction preserves the exact correspondence between normal-map zeros and VI solutions while changing numerical conditioning.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean normal map for a parameter-dependent convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(p\in P\) and \(z\in\mathbb R^n\), the parametric normal map associated with \(F\) and \(C\) is
\[
M(p,z):=F\bigl(p,\Pi_{C(p)}z\bigr)+z-\Pi_{C(p)}z.
\]
Writing \(x:=\Pi_{C(p)}z\), the projection characterization gives \(z-x\in N_{C(p)}(x)\). Consequently,
\[
M(p,z)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
-F(p,x)\in N_{C(p)}(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\langle F(p,x),y-x\rangle\geq0\quad\text{for every }y\in C(p).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameterized VI is equivalent to finding a zero of the normal map formed from its field and the projector onto its parameterized feasible set.
knowledge_statements.title: Parametric Normal Maps

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The variational inequality
\[
\langle \nabla f(x^*),x-x^*\rangle\geq0\quad\text{for every }x\in C
\]
is equivalent to \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\). Under the stated constraint qualification, this is further equivalent to the existence of multipliers \(\lambda_i\geq0\) and \(\mu_j\in\mathbb R\) such that
\[
\nabla f(x^*)+\sum_i\lambda_i\nabla g_i(x^*)+\sum_j\mu_j\nabla h_j(x^*)=0,
\quad g_i(x^*)\leq0,
\quad h_j(x^*)=0,
\quad \lambda_i g_i(x^*)=0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the VI field is a convex potential gradient, the VI is convex minimization and, under Slater's condition, reduces exactly to its KKT system.
knowledge_statements.title: Integrable-VI KKT Reduction

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
C:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:g_i(x)\leq0\ (i=1,\ldots,q),\ h_j(x)=0\ (j=1,\ldots,r)\}.
\]
A point \(x^*\in C\) solves \(\operatorname{VI}(C,F)\) if and only if there exist \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^q\) and \(\mu\in\mathbb R^r\) such that
\[
F(x^*)+\sum_{i=1}^q\lambda_i\nabla g_i(x^*)+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\nabla h_j(x^*)=0,
\qquad
\lambda_i g_i(x^*)=0\quad(i=1,\ldots,q).
\]
Primal feasibility is expressed by \(x^*\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex differentiable constraint system satisfying Slater's condition, the VI is equivalent to primal feasibility, stationarity, nonnegative inequality multipliers, unrestricted equality multipliers, and complementary slackness.
assumptions_latex: For \(i=1,\ldots,q\), \(g_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is convex and continuously differentiable.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order VI representation of finite-dimensional differentiable convex minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x^*\in C\),
\[
x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\langle\nabla f(x^*),x-x^*\rangle\geq0
\quad\text{for every }x\in C.
\]
Thus the optimization problem is represented by \(\operatorname{VI}(C,F)\) with \(F:=\nabla f\), equivalently by
\[
0\in\nabla f(x^*)+N_C(x^*).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Differentiable convex minimization over a closed convex set is equivalent to the VI whose field is the objective gradient.

children.title: Saddle Problems as VIs
children.top_down_role: VI representations arising from saddle-point problem structure.

assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) are nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\) is continuously differentiable, convex in \(x\), and concave in \(y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A pair is a saddle point of \(L\) exactly when it solves the VI on \(X\times Y\) with field \((\nabla_xL,-\nabla_yL)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional convex-concave saddle problems.

source_refs.locator: I.5 Some Problems Which Lead to Variational Inequalities p. 15
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A pair \((x^*,y^*)\in X\times Y\) is a saddle point when
\[
L(x^*,y)\leq L(x^*,y^*)\leq L(x,y^*)
\quad\text{for every }(x,y)\in X\times Y.
\]
Under convexity-concavity, this is equivalent to
\[
\left\langle\nabla_xL(x^*,y^*),x-x^*\right\rangle
-\left\langle\nabla_yL(x^*,y^*),y-y^*\right\rangle\geq0
\quad\text{for every }(x,y)\in X\times Y,
\]
which is \(\operatorname{VI}(X\times Y,F)\) for \(F(x,y):=(\nabla_xL(x,y),-\nabla_yL(x,y))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth convex-concave saddle point is precisely a VI solution for the primal gradient and negative dual gradient on the product set.
knowledge_statements.title: Saddle Problems as VIs

children.title: Optimization-to-Saddle Reduction Boundary
children.top_down_role: Structural distinctions between optimization-derived and saddle-derived VI representations.

assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable, but convexity is not assumed.
Stationarity is encoded as the unconstrained VI \(\nabla f(x^*)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without convexity, the optimization-to-VI or saddle first-order system can contain points that are not minimizers or saddle points.

notation.meaning: Nonconvex objective used in the boundary example

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of converse first-order reductions without convexity-concavity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the unconstrained problem with
\[
f(x):=(x^2-1)^2,
\qquad \nabla f(x)=4x(x^2-1).
\]
The point \(x^*=0\) satisfies the associated variational inequality on \(\mathbb R\), because \(\nabla f(0)=0\). Nevertheless, \(f(0)=1\) while \(f(1)=f(-1)=0\), and \(x^*=0\) is a strict local maximum. Hence a first-order VI, KKT, or degenerate saddle representation is not equivalent to global optimization after convexity is removed. Analogously, without convexity in the primal variable and concavity in the dual variable, saddle-gradient VI solutions need not satisfy the global saddle inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without convexity-concavity, first-order VI or saddle systems may admit stationary points that are neither minimizers nor saddle points.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimization-to-Saddle Reduction Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample correctly demonstrates failure of the optimization-to-VI converse without convexity, but the record supplies no inspectable source for the broader optimization-to-saddle boundary claim.

children.title: Nash Equilibria as VIs
children.top_down_role: VI formulations for strategic equilibrium systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Nash Equilibria as VIs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional differentiable convex games with uncoupled feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X:=\prod_{i=1}^N X_i\) and define
\[
F(x):=\bigl(\nabla_{x_1}J_1(x),\ldots,\nabla_{x_N}J_N(x)\bigr).
\]
A profile \(x^*\in X\) is a Nash equilibrium,
\[
J_i(x_i^*,x_{-i}^*)\leq J_i(x_i,x_{-i}^*)
\quad\text{for every }x_i\in X_i\text{ and }i=1,\ldots,N,
\]
if and only if
\[
\langle F(x^*),x-x^*\rangle\geq0
\quad\text{for every }x\in X.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a differentiable convex game with product constraints, Nash equilibria are exactly the solutions of the pseudo-gradient VI.
assumptions_latex: For \(i=1,\ldots,N\), the strategy set \(X_i\subseteq\mathbb R^{n_i}\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
Each \(J_i\) is continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(X:=\prod_{i=1}^N X_i\).
For every fixed \(x_{-i}\), the function \(x_i\mapsto J_i(x_i,x_{-i})\) is convex on \(X_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A profile is a Nash equilibrium exactly when it solves \(\operatorname{VI}(X,F)\).

notation.meaning: Cartesian product of player strategy sets

children.title: Network Equilibria as VIs
children.top_down_role: VI formulations for flow, traffic, and network equilibrium systems.

assumptions_latex: A directed network has a nonempty closed convex feasible flow set \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^A\).
The arc-cost map \(c:K\to\mathbb R^A\) is continuous.
Users are nonatomic and select feasible routes of minimum experienced cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible flow is a Wardrop equilibrium exactly when it solves \(\operatorname{VI}(K,c)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Static nonatomic routing equilibrium in arc-flow form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\) encode flow conservation, nonnegativity, and fixed origin-destination demands. A feasible flow \(x^*\in K\) is a Wardrop equilibrium when every used route has minimum cost among routes serving the same demand pair. In aggregate arc-flow variables this equilibrium condition is equivalent to
\[
\langle c(x^*),x-x^*\rangle
=\sum_{a\in A}c_a(x^*)(x_a-x_a^*)\geq0
\quad\text{for every }x\in K.
\]
Thus the network equilibrium is represented by \(\operatorname{VI}(K,c)\); uniqueness of the aggregate flow additionally follows when \(c\) is strictly monotone on \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Wardrop traffic equilibrium is the VI asserting that no feasible aggregate flow has lower cost in the equilibrium cost vector.
knowledge_statements.title: Network Equilibria as VIs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is supplied, and the route-based Wardrop condition requires explicit assumptions connecting route costs, arc costs, feasible path flows, and aggregate arc flows. The strict-monotonicity uniqueness claim also requires source support.

children.title: Network Games as VI Models
children.top_down_role: VI models combining strategic interaction with network structure.

assumptions_latex: Player \(i\) chooses a network action \(x_i\) from a nonempty closed convex set, with joint feasible set \(K\).
Each cost \(J_i(x_i,x_{-i})\) is differentiable and convex in the player's own action.
Shared network effects enter the costs or the joint feasible constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every variational network equilibrium solves the VI on \(K\) induced by the game pseudo-gradient.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex differentiable network games, including shared constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
F(x):=\bigl(\nabla_{x_1}J_1(x),\ldots,\nabla_{x_N}J_N(x)\bigr).
\]
A variational network equilibrium is a point \(x^*\in K\) satisfying
\[
\langle F(x^*),x-x^*\rangle
=\sum_i\left\langle\nabla_{x_i}J_i(x^*),x_i-x_i^*\right\rangle\geq0
\quad\text{for every }x\in K.
\]
When \(K=\prod_iX_i\), this condition is equivalent to Nash equilibrium under own-action convexity. For shared constraints, it selects the generalized Nash equilibria whose players use a common multiplier for the shared constraint system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex network game is modeled by the VI of its pseudo-gradient; shared constraints select the common-multiplier variational equilibrium.
knowledge_statements.title: Network Games as VI Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The product-set VI model is standard, but the shared-constraint claim about generalized Nash equilibria and common multipliers depends on a precise variational-equilibrium definition and constraint qualification. No inspectable source is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: VIs as Equilibrium Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional optimization with a parameterized VI constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An optimization problem with a variational-inequality equilibrium constraint has the form
\[
\operatorname*{minimize}_{x,y}\ \Phi(x,y)
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
x\in X,
\quad y\in K(x),
\quad \langle F(x,y),v-y\rangle\geq0\quad\text{for every }v\in K(x).
\]
Equivalently, its equilibrium constraint may be written as
\[
0\in F(x,y)+N_{K(x)}(y)
\]
or as \(y\in\operatorname{SOL}(K(x),F(x,\cdot))\). This equilibrium condition is part of the feasible-set definition of the upper-level problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An upper-level optimization problem has a VI equilibrium constraint when its lower-level variable is required to solve a parameterized VI.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is the upper-level feasible set.
For every \(x\in X\), \(K(x)\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(F:X\times\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^m\) defines the lower-level equilibrium field.
\(\Phi:X\times\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\) is the upper-level objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lower-level constraint requires \(y\in\operatorname{SOL}(K(x),F(x,\cdot))\), producing an optimization problem with a VI equilibrium constraint.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
Projection uses the Euclidean norm and inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Euclidean projector is single-valued, firmly nonexpansive, and characterized by a normal-cone inclusion.

notation.meaning: Euclidean projector onto the convex set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection onto a closed convex set in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(z\in\mathbb R^n\), there is a unique point
\[
P_C(z):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\|x-z\|.
\]
For \(x\in C\), the following conditions are equivalent:
\[
x=P_C(z),
\qquad z-x\in N_C(x),
\qquad \langle z-x,y-x\rangle\leq0\quad\text{for every }y\in C.
\]
Moreover, for all \(z,w\in\mathbb R^n\), the projector is firmly nonexpansive:
\[
\|P_Cz-P_Cw\|^2\leq\langle P_Cz-P_Cw,z-w\rangle.
\]
In particular, \(P_C\) is nonexpansive and hence globally Lipschitz with constant one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto a closed convex set is unique, firmly nonexpansive, and characterized by the residual belonging to the normal cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean Projector Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projection characterization and firm nonexpansiveness property are mathematically correct and the property kind fits the geometry leaf, but no inspectable authoritative source is supplied.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty polyhedral convex set.
\(\mathcal F(C)\) denotes the collection of nonempty faces of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cells \(F+N_C(F)\) form the polyhedral normal manifold, and projection onto \(C\) is affine on each cell.

notation.meaning: Normal cone constant on the relative interior of a face
Normal-manifold cell associated with a face

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Face-indexed normal manifold of a polyhedral convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each nonempty face \(F\in\mathcal F(C)\), let \(N_C(F)\) denote the normal cone \(N_C(x)\) at any \(x\in\operatorname{ri}F\), and define
\[
M_F:=F+N_C(F).
\]
The collection \(\{M_F:F\in\mathcal F(C)\}\) covers \(\mathbb R^n\), and the relative interiors of its full-dimensional cells are pairwise disjoint. If \(z\in M_F\), then \(P_C(z)\in F\); on every cell \(M_F\), the Euclidean projector \(P_C\) agrees with an affine mapping. Thus the face-normal pairs of \(C\) induce a polyhedral subdivision on which projection, and consequently a polyhedral normal map, is piecewise affine.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each face plus its normal cone forms a normal-manifold cell; these cells cover space and make polyhedral projection piecewise affine.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Manifold Decomposition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The face-normal cell description is plausible and fits the representation leaf, but the precise covering, cell-interior, and affine-projector assertions require an authoritative source with a specific locator.

assumptions_latex: \(C(p)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex for every \(p\in P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in C(p)}\frac12\|y-z\|^2=\{P_{C(p)}(z)\}=\{x\in C(p):\langle z-x,y-x\rangle\leq0\ \forall y\in C(p)\}.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(p\in P\) and \(z\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the projection \(P_{C(p)}(z)\) is the unique minimizer of \(y\mapsto \tfrac12\|y-z\|^2\) over \(C(p)\). A point \(x\in C(p)\) equals \(P_{C(p)}(z)\) if and only if \(\langle z-x,y-x\rangle\leq0\) for every \(y\in C(p)\), equivalently if and only if \(z-x\in N_{C(p)}(x)\). The characterization is pointwise in \(p\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A map \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}^q\) is piecewise affine if there are finitely many polyhedral sets \(Q_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), matrices \(A_i\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times n}\), and vectors \(b_i\in\mathbb{R}^q\) such that \(D=\bigcup_{i=1}^m Q_i\) and \(f(x)=A_i x+b_i\) whenever \(x\in Q_i\). Because \(f\) is single-valued, the affine formulas agree at every point belonging to overlapping cells.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A piecewise affine map has finitely many polyhedral domain cells and agrees with an affine formula on each cell.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A continuous map \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}^q\) is piecewise smooth, specifically piecewise \(C^1\), if for every \(\bar x\in D\) there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and finitely many maps \(f_i\in C^1(U;\mathbb{R}^q)\) such that \(f(x)\in\{f_1(x),\ldots,f_m(x)\}\) for every \(x\in U\cap D\). The active selection set at \(x\) is \(I(x)=\{i:f(x)=f_i(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous map is piecewise smooth when locally its value always equals one of finitely many continuously differentiable selection functions.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the normal map by \(F_C^{\mathrm{nor}}(z)=F(P_C(z))+z-P_C(z)\). For polyhedral \(C\) and continuously differentiable \(F\), this map is Bouligand differentiable. Writing \(x=P_C(z)\), the directional chain rule gives \(F_C^{\mathrm{nor}\,'}(z;h)=\nabla F(x)P_C'(z;h)+h-P_C'(z;h)\) for every \(h\in\mathbb{R}^n\). Hence its first-order model combines the smooth Jacobian of \(F\) with the critical-cone projector derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polyhedral normal map is Bouligand differentiable, and its derivative follows by combining the field Jacobian with the projector derivative.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a nonempty compact convex subset of \(\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(F:K\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuous. Then the variational inequality \(\operatorname{VI}(K,F)\) has at least one solution: there exists \(x^*\in K\) such that \(\langle F(x^*),y-x^*\rangle\geq0\) for every \(y\in K\). No monotonicity of \(F\) is required for this existence conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every continuous field on a nonempty compact convex finite-dimensional set has at least one variational-inequality solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Compact Convex Regime

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\alpha>0\), define \(T_\alpha:K\to K\) by \(T_\alpha(x)=P_K(x-\alpha F(x))\). The map \(T_\alpha\) is continuous and has a fixed point by Brouwer's fixed-point theorem. Moreover, \(x\in\operatorname{Fix}(T_\alpha)\) if and only if \(\langle F(x),y-x\rangle\geq0\) for every \(y\in K\). Thus \(\operatorname{Fix}(T_\alpha)=\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The projected field map is continuous, Brouwer guarantees a fixed point, and its fixed-point set is exactly the variational-inequality solution set.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Point Existence Route

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(y\in K\), set \(G(y)=\{x\in K:\langle F(x),y-x\rangle\geq0\}\). Each \(G(y)\) is closed, and \(G\) has the KKM covering property \(\operatorname{co}\{y_1,\ldots,y_m\}\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^mG(y_i)\). Since \(K\) is compact, the Fan–KKM lemma gives \(x^*\in\bigcap_{y\in K}G(y)\). Therefore \(\langle F(x^*),y-x^*\rangle\geq0\) for every \(y\in K\), so \(x^*\) solves \(\operatorname{VI}(K,F)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed-valued KKM correspondence formed from the VI inequalities has nonempty total intersection, and every intersection point solves the VI.
knowledge_statements.title: KKM Existence Route

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(t\in[0,1]\), let \(H_t(x)=H(x,t)\). If \(H_t(x)\neq0\) for every \((x,t)\in\partial\Omega\times[0,1]\), then every degree \(\deg(H_t,\Omega,0)\) is defined and is independent of \(t\). Hence a computable nonzero degree at \(t=0\) transfers to \(t=1\), forcing a zero of \(H_1\) in \(\Omega\). When each \(H_t\) is a VI residual, that zero is a solution of the terminal variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous deformation that never creates a boundary zero preserves degree, so a nonzero degree for a simple VI transfers to the target VI.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K^\infty=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:x+td\in K\text{ for every }x\in K, t\geq0\}\). If \(F\) is continuous and monotone and there exists \(x_0\in K\) such that \(\langle F(x_0),d\rangle>0\) for every \(d\in K^\infty\setminus\{0\}\), then the VI admits a solution. knowledge_statements.title: Browder–Minty Surjectivity Route
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coercive Browder–Minty route for constrained variational inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a real reflexive Banach space, let \(K\subseteq X\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(A:X\to X^*\) be monotone, hemicontinuous, and bounded on bounded sets. Suppose that for some \(u_0\in K\), \[\frac{\langle Au,u-u_0\rangle}{\lVert u\rVert}\longrightarrow +\infty\quad\text{as }u\in K,\ \lVert u\rVert\to\infty.\] Then, for every \(f\in X^*\), there exists \(u\in K\) such that \[\langle Au-f,v-u\rangle\geq0\qquad\text{for every }v\in K.\] Equivalently, \(f\in Au+N_K(u)\). If \(A\) is strictly monotone on \(K\), this solution is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coercive, monotone, hemicontinuous operator on a reflexive Banach space yields a solution of every corresponding constrained variational inequality; strict monotonicity additionally gives uniqueness.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real reflexive Banach space and \(K\subseteq X\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(A:X\to X^*\) is monotone, hemicontinuous, and bounded on bounded sets.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(f\in X^*\), there exists \(u\in K\) such that \(\langle Au-f,v-u\rangle\geq0\) for every \(v\in K\).

knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Monotonicity Uniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness only; existence must be supplied separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a nonempty convex subset of a real Hilbert space \(H\), and let \(F:K\to H\) be strictly monotone, meaning that \[\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle>0\qquad\text{whenever }x,y\in K\text{ and }x\neq y.\] Then the variational inequality for \(F\) on \(K\) has at most one solution: \[\lvert\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\rvert\leq1.\] Strict monotonicity alone does not ensure existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict monotonicity gives at most one variational-inequality solution but does not by itself ensure that a solution exists.

assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a nonempty closed convex subset of a Hilbert space.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x(p)\) denote the unique solution of the VI with map \(x\mapsto F(x)+p\). For all \(p,r\in H\), \[\lVert x(p)-x(r)\rVert\leq\frac{1}{\mu}\lVert p-r\rVert.\] Thus \(1/\mu\) controls absolute sensitivity to additive perturbations. When the scale of the forward operator is measured by its Lipschitz modulus \(L\), the dimensionless ratio \[\kappa:=\frac{L}{\mu}\] serves as the natural strong-monotonicity conditioning parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong monotonicity bounds additive-perturbation sensitivity by the reciprocal modulus; relative conditioning is measured by the Lipschitz-to-monotonicity ratio.

children.title: P-Function Conditions
children.top_down_role: Global uniqueness conditions based on the P-function property.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is a P-function on \(K\) exactly when the displayed strict maximum condition holds for every distinct pair.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional coordinatewise definition on an arbitrary domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) is a P-function on \(K\) if and only if, for every distinct \(x,y\in K\), \[\max_{1\le i\le n}(x_i-y_i)\bigl(F_i(x)-F_i(y)\bigr)>0.\] Equivalently, for every \(x\ne y\), at least one coordinate simultaneously gives a strictly positive displacement and operator-difference product.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mapping is a P-function when every distinct pair has at least one coordinate whose displacement and operator change have a strictly positive product.
knowledge_statements.title: P-Function Conditions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed condition is the standard finite-dimensional definition of a P-function and the condition role fits the leaf, but no inspectable citation or authoritative locator is supplied.

children.title: Uniform P-Function Conditions
children.top_down_role: Quantitatively strengthened P-function conditions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is uniformly P on \(K\) exactly when the displayed inequality holds for some \(\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic-growth version of the coordinatewise P condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) is a uniform P-function on \(K\) if and only if there exists \(\alpha>0\) such that, for all \(x,y\in K\), \[\max_{1\le i\le n}(x_i-y_i)\bigl(F_i(x)-F_i(y)\bigr)\ge \alpha\|x-y\|^2.\] Any admissible \(\alpha\) is a uniform P-function modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform P behavior requires the largest coordinate product to dominate the squared distance by one positive constant for every pair.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform P-Function Conditions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quadratic uniform P-function condition is precise and the condition role fits the leaf, but the record has no source supporting the selected normalization and definition.

children.title: Uniformity Strengthening Boundary
children.top_down_role: Structural distinction between ordinary and uniform P-function regimes.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is a P-function on \(K\) but is not a uniform P-function there.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete boundary showing that strict P behavior need not be uniform.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For distinct \(s,t\in K\), strict increase of \(F\) gives \((s-t)(s^3-t^3)>0\), so \(F\) is a P-function. Uniformity would require some \(\alpha>0\) satisfying \(t^4\ge\alpha t^2\) for every \(t\in K\), by comparing \(t\) with \(0\). This is impossible as nonzero \(t\to0\). Hence the implication uniform P \(\Rightarrow\) P is strict.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The scalar map t cubed is strictly P on a bounded interval but has no positive uniform P modulus near zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniformity Strengthening Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scalar example correctly separates P-function behavior from uniform P-function behavior and failure_boundary fits the terminal container. However, it has no citation and its statement includes a derivation rather than only the knowledge statement.

assumptions_latex: \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is a P-matrix, meaning every principal minor of \(M\) is positive.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the complementarity system \[z\ge0,\qquad w=Mz+q\ge0,\qquad \langle z,w\rangle=0.\] If \(M\) is a P-matrix, then for every \(q\in\mathbb{R}^n\) this system has a unique solution \(z\). Conversely, if the system has a unique solution for every \(q\in\mathbb{R}^n\), then \(M\) is a P-matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix is a P-matrix exactly when its linear complementarity problem has one and only one solution for every right-hand side.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The P-matrix characterization of unique solvability of LCP(M,q) for every right-hand side is a theorem matching this topic, but no authoritative theorem or page locator is cited.

children.title: P-Zero Relaxation
children.top_down_role: The weakened P-property regime based on P-zero behavior.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The P-zero condition is the nonstrict relaxation of the P-function condition.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise nonstrict relaxation of the P-function predicate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) is a P-zero function on \(K\) if, for every distinct \(x,y\in K\), \[\max_{1\le i\le n}(x_i-y_i)\bigl(F_i(x)-F_i(y)\bigr)\ge0.\] Replacing this nonstrict inequality by strict positivity yields the P-function condition; consequently every P-function is P-zero, but the reverse implication need not hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A P-zero function replaces the strict positive coordinate product required of a P-function by a nonnegative one.
knowledge_statements.title: P-Zero Relaxation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nonstrict coordinatewise condition correctly defines the finite-dimensional P-zero relaxation, and definition is appropriate for the leaf. No source or locator is provided.

children.title: Nonuniqueness Boundary
children.top_down_role: Regimes where global uniqueness can no longer be maintained.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and contains at least two points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is P-zero but not P, and every point of \(K\) solves \(\operatorname{VI}(K,F)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp loss of uniqueness after strict P positivity is removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any distinct \(x,y\in K\), every coordinate product \((x_i-y_i)(F_i(x)-F_i(y))\) equals \(0\). Thus \(F\) satisfies the P-zero condition but not the P-function condition. Moreover, every \(x\in K\) satisfies \[\langle F(x),y-x\rangle=0\qquad\text{for every }y\in K,\] so P-zero structure alone does not ensure uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The zero mapping is P-zero, yet every feasible point solves the variational inequality, showing exactly where P-based uniqueness can fail.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonuniqueness Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The zero-map example correctly marks the loss-of-uniqueness boundary and failure_boundary is the right role. The record lacks a citation, and the statement contains explanatory derivation that should not appear in a proof-free knowledge statement.

children.title: Multiplicity under P-Zero Structure

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The solution set is \(\{0\}\times[0,1]\), although \(F\) is P-zero.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonconstant P-zero mapping with a continuum of VI solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x,y\in K\), the coordinate products are \((x_1-y_1)^2\) and \(0\), so \(F\) is P-zero. The variational inequality is \[x_1(y_1-x_1)\ge0\qquad\text{for every }y_1\in[0,1].\] This holds exactly when \(x_1=0\), while \(x_2\) is unrestricted. Hence \[\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)=\{0\}\times[0,1].\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonconstant P-zero mapping on the unit square can have an entire line segment of variational-inequality solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: KKT-Triple Local Uniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth constrained VI; strong metric regularity gives local uniqueness of the entire primal-dual triple.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), \(h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p\), and \(z=(x,\lambda,\mu)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R_+^m\times\mathbb R^p\). Define \[\mathcal K(z):=\begin{pmatrix}F(x)+\nabla g(x)^\mathsf T\lambda+\nabla h(x)^\mathsf T\mu\\ h(x)\\-g(x)\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\N_{\mathbb R_+^m}(\lambda)\end{pmatrix}.\] If \(0\in\mathcal K(\bar z)\) and \(\mathcal K\) is strongly metrically regular at \((\bar z,0)\), then there are neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar z\) and \(V\) of \(0\) such that \(p\mapsto\mathcal K^{-1}(p)\cap U\) is single-valued and Lipschitz on \(V\). In particular, \(\mathcal K^{-1}(0)\cap U=\{\bar z\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong metric regularity of the KKT generalized equation makes the nearby primal-dual solution single-valued and Lipschitz, so the reference KKT triple is locally unique.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\), \(g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), and \(h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p\) are continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).
The feasible set is locally \(K=\{x:g(x)\leq0,\ h(x)=0\}\), and \(\bar z=(\bar x,\bar\lambda,\bar\mu)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R_+^m\times\mathbb R^p\) is a KKT triple.
The KKT generalized equation is strongly metrically regular at \((\bar z,0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There are neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar z\) and \(V\) of \(0\) such that every \(p\in V\) has exactly one solution \(z(p)\in U\), and \(p\mapsto z(p)\) is Lipschitz; hence \(\bar z\) is locally unique for \(p=0\).

notation.meaning: Perturbation of the KKT generalized equation.

knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Map Local Invertibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local-homeomorphism formulation for a finite-dimensional VI over a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(z\in\mathbb R^n\), define \[F_K^{\mathrm{nor}}(z):=F(\Pi_K z)+z-\Pi_K z.\] Suppose \(F_K^{\mathrm{nor}}(\bar z)=0\) and there are neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar z\) and \(V\) of \(0\) such that \(F_K^{\mathrm{nor}}:U\to V\) is a homeomorphism. Then \(\bar z\) is the unique zero in \(U\), and \(\bar x=\Pi_K(\bar z)\) is locally unique among solutions of \(0\in F(x)+N_K(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the normal map is a local homeomorphism at a zero, that zero and its corresponding nearby variational-inequality solution are locally unique.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
The normal map is a homeomorphism between a neighborhood of its zero \(\bar z\) and a neighborhood of \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The point \(\bar x=\Pi_K(\bar z)\) is the unique solution of \(0\in F(x)+N_K(x)\) in some neighborhood of \(\bar x\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The solution \(\bar x\) is normal-map nondegenerate if \[-F(\bar x)\in\operatorname{ri}N_K(\bar x).\] Writing \(\bar z=\bar x-F(\bar x)\), one has \(\Pi_K(\bar z)=\bar x\) and \(F_K^{\mathrm{nor}}(\bar z)=0\). knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonlinear complementarity formulation using absence of biactive indices, equivalently strict complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the complementarity system \[\bar x\geq0,\qquad \bar s=F(\bar x)\geq0,\qquad \bar x_i\bar s_i=0\quad(i=1,\ldots,n),\] define \(B(\bar x):=\{i:\bar x_i=0,\ \bar s_i=0\}\). The solution is complementarity nondegenerate when \[B(\bar x)=\varnothing.\] Equivalently, \(\bar x_i+\bar s_i>0\) for every index, so each complementary pair has exactly one positive component and the local active complementarity pattern is unambiguous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complementarity solution is nondegenerate when no pair has both components zero, equivalently every complementary pair has exactly one positive component.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(F:K\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuous and monotone. knowledge_statements.title: Connectedness of Solution Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Connectivity consequence of convexity for a nonempty continuous monotone VI solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(F:K\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuous and monotone. If \(\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\neq\varnothing\), then \(\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\) is path connected. More precisely, for all \(x^0,x^1\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\) and every \(t\in[0,1]\), \[(1-t)x^0+tx^1\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty solution set of a continuous monotone VI on a closed convex feasible set is path connected; the segment joining any two solutions remains in the solution set.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
The VI has at least one solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The solution set \(\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\) is path connected, and hence connected.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Connected Solution Sets

knowledge_statements.title: Disconnected Solution-Set Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete one-dimensional boundary mechanism showing that continuity alone does not ensure connected solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=[-2,2]\subset\mathbb R\) and define \(F:K\to\mathbb R\) by \(F(x)=x^2-1\). Then \[\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)=\{-2,-1,1\},\] which is disconnected. Thus continuity of \(F\) and convexity of \(K\) alone do not ensure connectedness of the VI solution set.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The VI solution set is \(\{-2,-1,1\}\), which is disconnected.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedrality of AVI Solution Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General affine VI over a polyhedron, with the monotone case distinguished.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty polyhedral convex set and let \(F(x)=Mx+q\). For every face \(G\) of \(K\), set \[S_G:=\{x\in G:-Mx-q\in N_K(G)\}.\] Then each \(S_G\) is a polyhedral convex set and \[\operatorname{SOL}(K,Mx+q)=\bigcup_{G\in\mathcal F(K)}S_G,\] where \(\mathcal F(K)\) is the finite face family of \(K\). If \(M\) is positive semidefinite, then the solution set is a convex polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine VI over a polyhedron has a solution set representable as a finite union of polyhedral face pieces; when the affine field is monotone, the complete solution set is a convex polyhedron.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty polyhedral convex set.
The VI field is affine: \(F(x)=Mx+q\), where \(M\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) and \(q\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The AVI solution set is a finite union of polyhedral convex sets; if \(M\) is positive semidefinite, it is a convex polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.title: Coercivity-Based Boundedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Radial coercivity condition proving boundedness, but not by itself existence, of VI solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and closed, let \(x^0\in K\), and let \(F:K\to\mathbb R^n\). Suppose there is \(R>0\) such that \[\langle F(x),x-x^0\rangle>0\qquad\text{for every }x\in K\text{ with }\lVert x\rVert>R.\] Then \[\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\subseteq K\cap\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\lVert x\rVert\leq R\}.\] Consequently, the solution set is bounded, although it may be empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the field points strictly outward relative to a fixed feasible point beyond a given radius, every VI solution lies within that radius; this condition does not itself ensure existence.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty and closed, and \(x^0\in K\).
\(F:K\to\mathbb R^n\) satisfies \(\langle F(x),x-x^0\rangle>0\) whenever \(x\in K\) and \(\lVert x\rVert>R\), for some \(R>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every solution of \(\operatorname{VI}(K,F)\) lies in \(K\cap\{x:\lVert x\rVert\leq R\}\); hence the solution set is bounded.

assumptions_latex: \(S:P\rightrightarrows X\) is a solution mapping between metric spaces and \(\bar x\in S(\bar p)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Semistability at \((\bar p,\bar x)\) means that every sequence \(p_k\to\bar p\) admits \(x_k\in S(p_k)\) with \(x_k\to\bar x\).
review_flags: Semistability has multiple conventions; an exact VI-specific source is needed to confirm this inner-persistence definition.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential inner-persistence convention for semistability of a parameterized solution mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The reference solution \(\bar x\in S(\bar p)\) is semistable if, for every sequence \(p_k\to\bar p\), there exist an index \(k_0\) and selections \(x_k\in S(p_k)\) for all \(k\ge k_0\) such that \(x_k\to\bar x\). Equivalently in metric spaces, \[\bar x\in\liminf_{p\to\bar p}S(p).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Semistability means every sufficiently small parameter sequence admits solutions converging to the designated reference solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Semistability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sequential condition is a valid inner-persistence property in metric spaces, but “semistability” has multiple inequivalent conventions. No VI-specific source identifies this as the intended definition.

children.title: Perturbed Solvability
children.top_down_role: Persistence of VI solvability under problem perturbations.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The VI is locally solvable under perturbation at \(\bar p\) when some neighborhood \(V\) of \(\bar p\) satisfies \(S(p)\ne\varnothing\) for every \(p\in V\).
review_flags: A source explicitly defining local perturbed solvability in this VI context is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local nonemptiness of every sufficiently small parameter perturbation of a finite-dimensional VI.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each parameter \(p\), define \[S(p):=\{x\in C(p):\langle F(x,p),y-x\rangle\ge0\ \text{for every }y\in C(p)\}.\] The reference VI is persistently solvable under small perturbations if there exists a neighborhood \(V\) of \(\bar p\) such that \(S(p)\ne\varnothing\) for every \(p\in V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Perturbed solvability means that every sufficiently small parameter perturbation retains at least one variational-inequality solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Perturbed Solvability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local nonemptiness definition is precise and fits the terminal container, but it has no cited source or explicit standard-field rationale.

children.title: Semistability-Based Solvability Persistence
children.top_down_role: Structural links between semistability and continued solvability.

assumptions_latex: \(S:P\rightrightarrows X\) is a solution mapping between metric spaces, \(\bar x\in S(\bar p)\), and \(\bar x\) is semistable in the sequential inner-persistence sense.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a neighborhood \(V\) of \(\bar p\) such that \(S(p)\ne\varnothing\) for every \(p\in V\).
review_flags: Depends on the selected semistability convention; an exact VI-specific source is needed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solvability consequence of sequential inner persistence in metric parameter spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose semistability holds at \((\bar p,\bar x)\). Then perturbed solvability must persist locally: there is a neighborhood \(V\) of \(\bar p\) for which \[S(p)\ne\varnothing\quad\text{for every }p\in V.\] Otherwise one could choose \(p_k\to\bar p\) with \(S(p_k)=\varnothing\), contradicting the semistability requirement that solutions \(x_k\in S(p_k)\) converge to \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential semistability forces all sufficiently small parameter perturbations to remain solvable.
knowledge_statements.title: Semistability-Based Solvability Persistence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The implication follows from the stated sequential inner-persistence convention in metric parameter spaces, but that convention for semistability remains unsupported. The final contradiction sentence is also proof text and should be removed once the result is sourced.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K:=T_C(\bar x)\cap F(\bar x,\bar p)^\perp\) and \(A:=\nabla_xF(\bar x,\bar p)\). children.title: Solution-Mapping Discontinuity

knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Mapping Discontinuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete finite-dimensional failure of lower semicontinuity caused by solution-set expansion at the reference parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(p\in\mathbb R\), define \(S(p)=\{x\in K:\langle F(x,p),y-x\rangle\geq0\text{ for every }y\in K\}\). Then \[S(p)=\begin{cases}\{-1\},&p>0,\\[-1,1],&p=0,\\\{1\},&p<0.\end{cases}\] The mapping \(S\) is outer semicontinuous but not lower semicontinuous, and hence not Painlevé--Kuratowski continuous, at \(p=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For this linear VI on an interval, every feasible point is a solution at zero, whereas only an endpoint is a solution at each nonzero nearby parameter; the solution map is outer semicontinuous but not lower semicontinuous at zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is not lower semicontinuous at \(p=0\), although it is outer semicontinuous there.

knowledge_statements.title: Degeneracy-Induced Discontinuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar generalized-equation example in which singular linearization coincides with loss of nearby solvability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The variational inequality is equivalent to \(x^2+p=0\), and its solution mapping is \[S(p)=\begin{cases}\{-\sqrt{-p},\sqrt{-p}\},&p<0,\\\{0\},&p=0,\\\varnothing,&p>0.\end{cases}\] At \((x,p)=(0,0)\), \(D_xF(0,0)=0\). The solution mapping has no nonempty-valued localization on a full neighborhood of \(p=0\); local solvability, a calm single-valued localization, and the Aubin property therefore fail at \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the equation x squared plus p equals zero, the singular solution at zero disappears under every positive perturbation, so local solvability and the stated stable-localization properties fail.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The degenerate solution at \(p=0\) is destroyed by every sufficiently small positive perturbation.

knowledge_statements.title: KKT-Triple Error Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local residual bound for smooth inequality-and-equality constrained VI KKT systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(z=(x,\lambda,\mu)\), define \[R_{\rm KKT}(z)=\bigl(F(x)+\nabla g(x)^\top\lambda+\nabla h(x)^\top\mu,\ h(x),\ \min\{\lambda,-g(x)\}\bigr),\] where the minimum is componentwise, and let \(Z^*=\{z:\lambda\geq0,\ R_{\rm KKT}(z)=0\}\). A local KKT-triple error bound at \(\bar z\in Z^*\) holds if there exist \(\kappa>0\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(z,Z^*)\leq\kappa\|R_{\rm KKT}(z)\|\] whenever \(\lambda\geq0\) and \(\|z-\bar z\|<\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a reference KKT triple, a KKT-triple error bound controls distance to the KKT-triple set by the stationarity, feasibility, and complementarity residual.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\), \(g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), and \(h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^q\) are continuously differentiable.
\((\bar x,\bar\lambda,\bar\mu)\) is a KKT triple with \(\bar\lambda\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A KKT-triple error bound is \(\operatorname{dist}(z,Z^*)\leq\kappa\|R_{\rm KKT}(z)\|\) locally around \(\bar z\).

knowledge_statements.title: Linearly Constrained Composite-VI Error Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized-equation error bound for a convex composite VI over linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(z=(x,\lambda)\), define \[H(z)=\bigl(F(x)+\partial g(x)+A^\top\lambda,\ b-Ax+N_{\mathbb R_+^m}(\lambda)\bigr).\] The inclusion \(0\in H(z)\) represents the composite VI condition \(0\in F(x)+\partial g(x)+N_C(x)\) together with a compatible multiplier. If \(H\) is metrically subregular at \((\bar z,0)\), then there exist \(\kappa>0\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(z,H^{-1}(0))\leq\kappa\operatorname{dist}(0,H(z))\] whenever \(\|z-\bar z\|<\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric subregularity of the composite primal-dual KKT mapping bounds local solution distance by its stationarity and linear-complementarity residual.
assumptions_latex: \(g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex, and \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) is continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Metric subregularity of \(H\) at \((\bar z,0)\) yields \(\operatorname{dist}(z,H^{-1}(0))\leq\kappa\operatorname{dist}(0,H(z))\) locally.

knowledge_statements.title: Monotone VI Global Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak-sharpness global bound for a finite-dimensional monotone VI using the primal gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(G(x)=\sup_{y\in K}\langle F(x),x-y\rangle\) and let \(S\) be the VI solution set. If there exists \(\alpha>0\) such that \(\langle F(x^*),x-x^*\rangle\geq\alpha\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\) for every \(x\in K\) and every \(x^*\in P_S(x)\), then \[\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\frac{G(x)}{\alpha}\qquad\text{for every }x\in K.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuous monotone VI satisfying the stated weak-sharpness condition, the primal gap globally bounds distance to the solution set with constant one over the sharpness modulus.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(F:K\to\mathbb R^n\) is continuous and monotone.
The VI solution set \(S\) is nonempty, and the primal gap \(G(x)\) is finite for every \(x\in K\).
For some \(\alpha>0\), every \(x\in K\) and every \(x^*\in P_S(x)\) satisfy \(\langle F(x^*),x-x^*\rangle\geq\alpha\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x\in K\), \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq G(x)/\alpha\).
