knowledge_statements.title: Potential-Reduction Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interior logarithmic-potential reduction template for nonlinear complementarity equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\rho>0\), define \[\Phi_\rho(x,y)=(n+\rho)\log(x^Ty)-\sum_{i=1}^n\log(x_iy_i)\] on strictly positive pairs. At an interior iterate \((x^k,y^k)\), compute a Newton-type direction from the linearization of \(F(x)-y=0\) together with a positively perturbed complementarity equation \(Xy=\tau_ke\), where \(\tau_k>0\). Select a step length that preserves \(x^{k+1}>0\) and \(y^{k+1}>0\), and accept it only when the prescribed potential-and-feasibility merit test decreases. Stop when both \(\|F(x^k)-y^k\|\) and \((x^k)^Ty^k\) do not exceed \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute a Newton step for feasibility and positively perturbed complementarity, shorten it to preserve strict positivity, and accept it only under the chosen potential-and-feasibility decrease test.
assumptions_latex: The nonlinear complementarity problem is \(x\geq0\), \(y=F(x)\geq0\), and \(x^Ty=0\).
Every trial step begins from a strictly interior pair \(x>0\), \(y>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accepted update preserves strict positivity and satisfies the prescribed potential-and-feasibility merit decrease; no convergence-to-zero conclusion is asserted without additional global assumptions.

Update the pair and stop when feasibility and complementarity residuals do not exceed \(\varepsilon\).

children.title: Interior Path-Following
children.top_down_role: Path-following methods whose trajectories remain in the interior regime.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is closed, convex, has nonempty interior, and admits a differentiable barrier \(B:\operatorname{int}K\to\mathbb{R}\).
\(F:K\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is continuous, and each selected barrier equation has a solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_k\in\operatorname{int}K\) for every \(k\), and every accumulation point satisfying \(\mu_k\downarrow0\) and \(r_k\to0\) solves \(0\in F(x)+N_K(x)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(x_0\in\operatorname{int}K\), parameters \(\mu_k\downarrow0\), and tolerances \(\eta_k\downarrow0\). At stage \(k\), compute \(x_k\in\operatorname{int}K\) satisfying \[r_k=F(x_k)+\mu_k\nabla B(x_k),\qquad \|r_k\|\leq\eta_k.\] Reduce \(\mu_k\) only after the current residual test holds, and output the final \(x_k\) or an accumulation point. This follows the barrier central path while retaining strict feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximately solve successive barrier equations with decreasing barrier parameters while keeping every iterate strictly feasible; vanishing residuals and parameters identify a VI solution.

children.title: Path-Regime Transition Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural boundaries between interior and noninterior trajectories.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is closed, convex, and has nonempty interior.
\(R_\mu:D_\mu\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is the parameterized equation used by the path method.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regime is interior precisely when \(D_\mu\subseteq\operatorname{int}K\) and the update preserves \(x_k\in D_{\mu_k}\) for every \(\mu_k>0\); it is noninterior when admissible iterates may lie in \(\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\operatorname{int}K\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(\mu>0\), inspect the domain \(D_\mu\) and the invariant set of the update solving \(R_\mu(x)=0\). Loss of either domain containment \(D_\mu\subseteq\operatorname{int}K\) or strict-feasibility invariance marks the transition from interior to noninterior path-following. Merely having feasible limit points does not make a path interior; strict feasibility must hold at every positive parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A path is interior only while its residual domain and updates enforce strict feasibility at every positive parameter; otherwise it belongs to the noninterior regime.

assumptions_latex: For the vector extension, \(u,v\in\mathbb{R}^q\) for an integer \(q\geq1\), and inequalities and products are interpreted componentwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(\mu>0\), \(\phi_\mu\) is continuously differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}^2\); moreover, \(\phi_\mu(a,b)\to\phi_0(a,b)\) as \(\mu\downarrow0\), and \(\phi_0(a,b)=0\) if and only if \(a\geq0\), \(b\geq0\), and \(ab=0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(a,b\in\mathbb{R}\) and \(\mu\geq0\), define \[\phi_\mu(a,b)=\sqrt{a^2+b^2+2\mu^2}-a-b.\] For \(\mu>0\), this function is continuously differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}^2\). As \(\mu\downarrow0\), it converges pointwise to \(\phi_0\), and \(\phi_0(a,b)=0\) holds exactly when \(a\geq0\), \(b\geq0\), and \(ab=0\). For \(u,v\in\mathbb{R}^q\), define \(\Phi_\mu(u,v)_i=\phi_\mu(u_i,v_i)\) for \(i=1,\ldots,q\); then the limiting equation \(\Phi_0(u,v)=0\) represents componentwise complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The smoothed Fischer-Burmeister function replaces each scalar complementarity pair by a smooth equation. Applied componentwise, its zero system converges to the original finite-dimensional complementarity system as the smoothing parameter vanishes.

For every \(\mu\in(0,\bar\mu]\) on the tracked path, \(\nabla_xH(x(\mu),\mu)\) is nonsingular, and the damped Newton stages produce accepted points satisfying their prescribed residual tolerances.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(\mu_0\in(0,\bar\mu]\), a reduction factor \(\theta\in(0,1)\), and tolerances \(\eta_k\downarrow0\). At stage \(k\), start from the preceding accepted point and apply damped Newton corrections \[\nabla_xH(z,\mu_k)d=-H(z,\mu_k),\qquad z\leftarrow z+\alpha d,\qquad \alpha\in(0,1],\] until an accepted point \(x_k=z\) satisfies \(\|H(x_k,\mu_k)\|\leq\eta_k\). Set \(\mu_{k+1}=\theta\mu_k\) and repeat. If the accepted sequence has an accumulation point \(\bar x\), continuity of \(H\) at parameter zero and the vanishing stage residuals give \(H(\bar x,0)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each decreasing smoothing parameter, use damped Newton corrections to meet a vanishing residual tolerance. Any accumulation point of the accepted stage points solves the continuously extended limiting equation.
knowledge_statements.title: Continuation-Based Smoothing

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(F:C\to\mathbb{R}^n\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x,y\in C\), define \[D_h(y,x)=h(y)-h(x)-\langle\nabla h(x),y-x\rangle\] and, for any \(\lambda>0\), \[T(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in C}\left\{\lambda\langle F(x),y\rangle+D_h(y,x)\right\}.\] Then \(x^\star\in C\) satisfies \(\langle F(x^\star),y-x^\star\rangle\geq0\) for every \(y\in C\) exactly when \(T(x^\star)=x^\star\). Thus the VI is reduced to the equation \(x-T(x)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A VI solution is exactly a fixed point of the Bregman proximal map obtained by minimizing a linearized operator term plus Bregman divergence.
knowledge_statements.title: Bregman-Based Reduction Methods

children.title: Exterior Barrier Reductions
children.top_down_role: Equation reductions based on exterior barrier constructions.

assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuous, and solutions of the penalized equations remain bounded as \(\rho\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any accumulation point with vanishing violation solves the original VI when the limiting multiplier \(\nu=\lim\rho(Gx-h)_+\) exists and satisfies stationarity and complementarity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exterior penalty interpretation; the taxonomy’s barrier terminology requires confirmation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\rho>0\), permit inequality-infeasible trial points and solve the exterior reduction \[F(x)+A^\top\lambda+G^\top\nu_\rho(x)=0,
\qquad Ax=b,\qquad \nu_\rho(x)=\rho(Gx-h)_+.\] Increase \(\rho\) and terminate when both the equation residual and \(\|(Gx-h)_+\|\) meet prescribed tolerances. Unlike an interior barrier equation, this residual is defined on infeasible points and drives violations toward zero through an exterior penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exterior reduction allows infeasible iterates and penalizes positive constraint violations increasingly strongly until feasibility and stationarity are recovered.
knowledge_statements.title: Exterior Barrier Reductions

children.title: Barrier-Regime Comparison
children.top_down_role: Structural comparison of interior and exterior reduction regimes.

assumptions_latex: The interior system uses \(s>0\), \(\nu>0\), and \(\nu\odot s=\mu\mathbf1\).
The exterior system uses \(\nu_\rho=\rho(Gx-h)_+\) and permits violated inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regimes have the same target KKT-complementarity system but different finite-parameter domains: strict feasibility for the interior regime and possible infeasibility for the exterior regime.

notation.meaning: interior barrier parameter tending to zero
exterior penalty parameter tending to infinity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-parameter domain and limiting-system comparison of the two reduction regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For positive finite parameters, the interior reduction is defined only with \(h-Gx>0\) and approaches active constraints from within \(C\). The exterior reduction remains defined when \(Gx>h\) and suppresses violations as \(\rho\to\infty\). Under boundedness and consistency of their induced multipliers, both limiting processes yield \[F(x)+A^\top\lambda+G^\top\nu=0,\qquad Ax=b,\qquad 0\leq\nu\perp h-Gx\geq0.\] They therefore differ in path geometry, not in the target complementarity system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interior reductions maintain strict feasibility, whereas exterior reductions may violate constraints; under consistency assumptions, both converge to the same KKT-complementarity system.
knowledge_statements.title: Barrier-Regime Comparison

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The comparison is coherent only after interpreting the exterior sibling as the proposed penalty method. children.title: Pointwise Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Guarantees attached to individually selected iterates.

assumptions_latex: An algorithm generates \(x_0,\ldots,x_N\in C\) for a VI on \(C\).
\(R:C\to[0,\infty]\) is a specified residual with \(R(x)=0\) exactly at solutions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The run has an \(N\)-step pointwise guarantee at level \(\varepsilon_N\) when \(\min_{0\leq k\leq N}R(x_k)\leq\varepsilon_N\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Best-individual-iterate output guarantee, distinct from averaging and terminal output.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an iteration budget \(N\), select \[k_N\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{0\leq k\leq N}R(x_k)\] and output \(x_{k_N}\). A pointwise complexity statement is a bound \[R(x_{k_N})=\min_{0\leq k\leq N}R(x_k)\leq\varepsilon_N.\] Equivalently, achieving tolerance \(\varepsilon\) requires at most the least \(N\) for which \(\varepsilon_N\leq\varepsilon\), with one iteration counted according to the declared oracle model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pointwise guarantee certifies that at least one individual iterate among the first N has small residual and outputs the best such iterate.

children.title: Last-Iterate Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Guarantees attached specifically to the terminal iterate.

assumptions_latex: An algorithm generates \(x_0,\ldots,x_N\in C\) for a VI on \(C\).
\(R:C\to[0,\infty]\) is a specified residual with \(R(x)=0\) exactly at solutions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The run has an \(N\)-step last-iterate guarantee at level \(\varepsilon_N\) precisely when \(R(x_N)\leq\varepsilon_N\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminal-iterate output guarantee without best-iterate selection or averaging.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: After exactly \(N\) declared oracle iterations, output the terminal point \(x_N\). A last-iterate complexity statement has the form \[R(x_N)\leq\varepsilon_N.\] Consequently, tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\) is reached within the least budget \(N\) satisfying \(\varepsilon_N\leq\varepsilon\). This requirement is stronger than the corresponding pointwise assertion \(\min_{0\leq k\leq N}R(x_k)\leq\varepsilon_N\), because it certifies the prescribed terminal output itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A last-iterate guarantee bounds the VI residual of the terminal iterate itself, without selecting an earlier or averaged output.
knowledge_statements.title: Last-Iterate Guarantees

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record accurately distinguishes a terminal residual condition from a best-iterate condition, but an arbitrary sequence epsilon_N without an algorithm, rate, residual, or oracle model is a definition or condition rather than a complexity bound. an index attaining the smallest observed residual

knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is a best-iterate certificate, not by itself an iteration-complexity rate or a last-iterate guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N\in\mathbb{N}\). Given iterates \(x_0,\ldots,x_N\), errors \(r_k\ge 0\), and weights \(w_k>0\), suppose \(\sum_{k=0}^{N}w_kr_k\le E_N\). For any \(k_*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{0\le k\le N}r_k\), \[r_{k_*}=\min_{0\le k\le N}r_k\le \frac{\sum_{k=0}^{N}w_kr_k}{\sum_{k=0}^{N}w_k}\le \frac{E_N}{\sum_{k=0}^{N}w_k}.\] Therefore the first \(N+1\) iterates contain an output with error at most \(\varepsilon\) whenever \(E_N\le\varepsilon\sum_{k=0}^{N}w_k\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the weighted-average guarantee for the dual gap, which is convex in its iterate argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For generated points \(x_0,\ldots,x_N\in C\) and weights \(w_k>0\), define \(W_N=\sum_{k=0}^{N}w_k\) and \(\bar x_N=W_N^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{N}w_kx_k\). Because \(g_D(x)=\sup_{y\in C}\langle F(y),x-y\rangle\) is a supremum of affine functions of \(x\), it is convex. Consequently, \[g_D(\bar x_N)\le \frac{1}{W_N}\sum_{k=0}^{N}w_kg_D(x_k).\] Hence any cumulative estimate \(\sum_{k=0}^{N}w_kg_D(x_k)\le E_N\) yields the ergodic certificate \(g_D(\bar x_N)\le E_N/W_N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual gap at a weighted average of iterates is at most the weighted average of their dual gaps.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An exact operator-evaluation oracle for \(F:C\to\mathbb{R}^d\) is a mapping \(\mathcal{O}_F\) that, on every admissible query \(x\in C\), returns \[\mathcal{O}_F(x)=F(x).\] The algorithm may choose each query adaptively from previous oracle responses and internal computations. knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Every Q-matrix is Q-zero, because solvability for all \(q\in\mathbb R^n\) implies solvability whenever feasibility holds. The inclusion is strict. For \(n=1\), let \(M=[0]\). If \(q\ge0\), then \(x=0\) solves the LCP; if \(q<0\), the inequality \(Mx+q\ge0\) is infeasible. Hence \([0]\in Q_0\). However, for \(q=-1\), no LCP solution exists, so \([0]\notin Q\). Therefore
\[
Q\subsetneq Q_0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every Q-matrix is Q-zero, but the inclusion is strict: the scalar zero matrix is Q-zero and is not a Q-matrix.

M\in P_0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \det(M_{II})\ge0\quad\text{for every nonempty }I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}.
\]
Unlike a P-matrix, a P-zero matrix may have zero diagonal entries, a zero determinant, or other vanishing principal minors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real square matrix is P-zero when every nonempty principal minor is nonnegative; zero principal minors are permitted.
knowledge_statements.title: P-Zero Matrices

children.title: P-Class Inclusion Boundary
children.top_down_role: Structural relationship between the P and P-zero classes.

assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(P_0\) denote the real P-matrix and P-zero matrix classes of a fixed order \(n\ge1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\subsetneq P_0\) and \(\overline P=P_0\).

notation.meaning: Closure in the Euclidean topology of \(\mathbb R^{n\times n}\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes both strict inclusion and the topological boundary obtained by relaxing strict principal-minor inequalities.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 3, P-matrices and P-zero matrices; exact subsection pending
source_refs.source_title: The Linear Complementarity Problem

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Strict positivity of all principal minors implies their nonnegativity, so \(P\subseteq P_0\). The inclusion is strict because the zero matrix belongs to \(P_0\) but not to \(P\). Moreover, continuity of principal minors gives \(\overline P\subseteq P_0\), while for every \(M\in P_0\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), the matrix \(M+\varepsilon I_n\) is a P-matrix and converges to \(M\) as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\). Consequently,
\[
P\subsetneq P_0=\overline P.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: P-matrices form a strict subset of P-zero matrices, and the P-zero class is exactly the closure of the P-matrix class.
knowledge_statements.title: P-Class Inclusion Boundary

children.title: Sufficient Matrices
children.top_down_role: LCP structure governed by sufficient matrix classes.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\) is sufficient exactly when both \(M\) and \(M^\top\) satisfy the displayed componentwise implication.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the standard LCP definition: sufficient means both column sufficient and row sufficient.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 3, sufficient matrices; exact subsection pending

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The matrix \(M\) is column sufficient when
\[
\forall x\in\mathbb R^n,\\ \bigl[x_i(Mx)_i\le0\ \text{for every }i\bigr]\Longrightarrow\bigl[x_i(Mx)_i=0\ \text{for every }i\bigr].
\]
It is row sufficient when \(M^\top\) is column sufficient. It is a sufficient matrix when it is both row and column sufficient. Equivalently, both \(M\) and \(M^\top\) obey the preceding componentwise implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix is sufficient when it and its transpose forbid a nonzero componentwise product whose entries are all nonpositive.

children.title: Copositive Matrices
children.top_down_role: LCP structure governed by copositive matrix classes.

assumptions_latex: \(M\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\); symmetry is not required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\) is copositive exactly when \(x^\top Mx\ge0\) for every \(x\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Copositivity is imposed only on the nonnegative orthant, not on all vectors.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 3, copositive matrices and complementarity; exact subsection pending

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A real square matrix \(M\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is copositive if
\[
x^\top Mx\ge0\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb R_+^n.
\]
Because \(x^\top Mx=x^\top\bigl((M+M^\top)/2\bigr)x\), copositivity depends only on the symmetric part of \(M\). Positive semidefiniteness implies copositivity, but copositivity tests the quadratic form only on \(\mathbb R_+^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix is copositive when its quadratic form is nonnegative on every vector in the nonnegative orthant.
knowledge_statements.title: Copositive Matrices

children.title: Sufficiency–Copositivity Relations
children.top_down_role: Inclusions, overlaps, and separations between the two classes.

assumptions_latex: Matrix classes are interpreted over real square matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Neither sufficiency nor copositivity implies the other.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete two-dimensional examples show that the sufficient and copositive classes are incomparable.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 3, sufficient and copositive matrix classes; exact subsection pending
source_refs.source_title: The Linear Complementarity Problem

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The sufficient and copositive classes are incomparable. The matrix \(C=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\) is copositive because \(x^\top Cx=2x_1x_2\ge0\) for \(x\ge0\), but with \(x=(1,-1)^\top\) one has \(x_i(Cx)_i=-1\) for both indices, so \(C\) is not column sufficient. Conversely, \(S=\begin{pmatrix}1&-10\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\) is a P-matrix and hence sufficient, while
\[
(1,1)S(1,1)^\top=-8<0,
\]
so \(S\) is not copositive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sufficiency and copositivity are incomparable: explicit two-by-two matrices satisfy either property without satisfying the other.
knowledge_statements.title: Sufficiency–Copositivity Relations

children.title: Semimonotone Matrices
children.top_down_role: LCP geometry associated with semimonotone matrices.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\) is semimonotone exactly when every nonzero \(x\ge0\) has an active index \(i\) with \((Mx)_i\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the standard complementarity-theory class \(E_0\), also called semimonotone.

source_refs.locator: §3.9 Semimonotone and Regular Matrices, p. 184

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A real square matrix \(M\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is semimonotone, written \(M\in E_0\), if
\[
\forall x\in\mathbb R_+^n\setminus\{0\},\quad \exists i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\quad x_i>0\quad\text{and}\quad (Mx)_i\ge0.
\]
Thus the restriction of \(Mx\) to the positive support of any nonzero nonnegative vector cannot be strictly negative in every component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix is semimonotone when every nonzero nonnegative vector has a positive component whose corresponding image component is nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.title: Semimonotone Matrices

children.title: Regular Matrices
children.top_down_role: LCP geometry associated with regular matrices.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\) is regular when some \(d>0\) makes the displayed augmented complementarity system trivial in \(x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the complementarity-theoretic regular-matrix convention associated with an augmented LCP system.

source_refs.locator: §3.9 Semimonotone and Regular Matrices, p. 184
source_refs.source_title: The Linear Complementarity Problem

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A matrix \(M\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is regular in the complementarity sense if there exists \(d\in\mathbb R^n\) with \(d>0\) such that every pair \((x,t)\in\mathbb R_+^n\times\mathbb R_+\) satisfying
\[
Mx+td\ge0,\qquad x^\top(Mx+td)=0
\]
has \(x=0\). The scalar \(t\) need not be zero; the condition rules out nonzero complementary vectors throughout the positive-reference homotopy generated by \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complementarity-regular matrix admits a positive reference vector for which the associated augmented homogeneous complementarity system has no nonzero vector solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Regular Matrices

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\) is a Z-matrix exactly when \(m_{ij}\le0\) for all \(i\ne j\).

A real square matrix \(M=(m_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is a Z-matrix if
\[
m_{ij}\le0\qquad\text{whenever }i\ne j.
\]
There is no sign restriction on the diagonal entries. Equivalently, \(M\) can be represented as \(M=sI_n-B\), where \(B\ge0\) entrywise and \(s\in\mathbb R\).

children.title: Matrix-Class Intersection Regimes
children.top_down_role: Overlaps and separations among the three matrix classes.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Within the Z-class, \(M\in P\) is equivalent to \(M\) being a nonsingular M-matrix, and \(M\in P_0\) is equivalent to being an M-matrix.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the classical P/P-zero intersections with Z-matrices through M-matrix spectral representations.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 3, intersections of Z-, P-, and P-zero matrix classes; exact subsection pending
source_refs.source_title: The Linear Complementarity Problem

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M\) be a Z-matrix. Then the following class intersections hold:
\[
M\in P\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad M=sI_n-B\ \text{for some }B\ge0\text{ and }s>\rho(B),
\]
and
\[
M\in P_0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad M=sI_n-B\ \text{for some }B\ge0\text{ and }s\ge\rho(B).
\]
Thus \(Z\cap P\) is the class of nonsingular M-matrices, whereas \(Z\cap P_0\) is the class of possibly singular M-matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Among Z-matrices, P-matrices are precisely nonsingular M-matrices, while P-zero matrices are precisely M-matrices, including singular ones.
knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Class Intersection Regimes

children.title: Global LCP Existence
children.top_down_role: Global regimes concerning the presence of LCP solutions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{SOL}(M,q)\neq\varnothing\) for every \(q\in\mathbb{R}^n\) if and only if \(M\) is a \(Q\)-matrix.

notation.meaning: solution set of the linear complementarity problem
matrix whose LCP is solvable for every right-hand side

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines global existence through the standard finite-dimensional \(Q\)-matrix class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) and \(q\in\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(\operatorname{SOL}(M,q)\) contain all pairs represented by \(z\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfying \(z\geq0\), \(w=Mz+q\geq0\), and \(z^{\mathsf T}w=0\). Global LCP existence means that \(\operatorname{SOL}(M,q)\neq\varnothing\) for every \(q\in\mathbb{R}^n\). A matrix has this property exactly when it belongs to the class of \(Q\)-matrices; equivalently, the predicate defining that class is universal solvability of \(\operatorname{LCP}(M,q)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An LCP matrix has global existence precisely when its complementarity problem has a solution for every right-hand side; such matrices are called Q-matrices.
knowledge_statements.title: Global LCP Existence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Q-matrix characterization is mathematically standard and fits the global-existence condition leaf, but no source or inspectable locator is supplied.

children.title: Global LCP Uniqueness
children.top_down_role: Global regimes concerning uniqueness of LCP solutions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{SOL}(M,q)\) is a singleton for every \(q\in\mathbb{R}^n\) if and only if every principal minor of \(M\) is positive.

notation.meaning: solution set of the LCP with matrix M and vector q
matrix with all principal minors positive

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the classical finite-dimensional global uniqueness theorem for LCPs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\). The problem \(z\geq0\), \(Mz+q\geq0\), and \(z^{\mathsf T}(Mz+q)=0\) has exactly one solution \(z\) for every \(q\in\mathbb{R}^n\) if and only if \(M\) is a \(P\)-matrix, meaning that every principal minor of \(M\) is positive. Thus the universal uniqueness property depends only on \(M\), not on a particular right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An LCP has exactly one solution for every right-hand side if and only if its matrix is a P-matrix.
knowledge_statements.title: Global LCP Uniqueness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-dimensional P-matrix equivalence is the correct theorem for global LCP uniqueness, but it has no cited source or specific locator.

children.title: Existence–Uniqueness Matrix-Class Links
children.top_down_role: Matrix-class structure connecting the two global solution properties.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\in P\Rightarrow M\in Q\), while \(M\in Q\) need not imply \(M\in P\).

notation.meaning: class of matrices with all principal minors positive
class of matrices giving a solvable LCP for every right-hand side

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates universal existence and universal uniqueness matrix classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), membership in the \(P\)-matrix class is equivalent to unique solvability of \(\operatorname{LCP}(M,q)\) for every \(q\in\mathbb{R}^n\). Consequently every \(P\)-matrix is a \(Q\)-matrix, because uniqueness includes existence. The reverse implication fails in general: universal existence alone does not force positive principal minors or universal uniqueness. Hence \(P\subsetneq Q\) in dimensions where \(Q\)-matrices outside \(P\) exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every P-matrix is a Q-matrix because universal uniqueness implies universal existence, but a Q-matrix need not provide uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.title: Existence–Uniqueness Matrix-Class Links

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The class relation P⊊Q is appropriate to this leaf and follows from the two global properties, but the strict inclusion and reverse-implication failure require sourced support.

children.title: LCP Nondegeneracy
children.top_down_role: Local LCP structure associated with nondegenerate solutions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z\) is nondegenerate exactly when \(z_i+w_i>0\) for every \(i\).

notation.meaning: indices with positive primal complementarity variable

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses solution-level nondegeneracy, equivalently strict complementarity.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.2 Conditions for local uniqueness p. 271
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z\in\operatorname{SOL}(M,q)\) and set \(w=Mz+q\). Define \(\alpha=\{i:z_i>0\}\), \(\beta=\{i:w_i>0\}\), and \(\gamma=\{i:z_i=w_i=0\}\). The solution is nondegenerate in the solution-level LCP sense when \(\gamma=\varnothing\). Equivalently, exactly one member of each complementary pair \((z_i,w_i)\) is positive, so \(z_i+w_i>0\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An LCP solution is nondegenerate when no complementary pair has both entries zero; equivalently, strict complementarity holds at every index.
knowledge_statements.title: LCP Nondegeneracy

children.title: Local LCP Uniqueness
children.top_down_role: Local regimes concerning isolation of an LCP solution.

knowledge_statements.title: Local LCP Uniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States an active-set criterion for isolated local uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), \(q\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(z^*\in\operatorname{SOL}(M,q)\), and put \(w^*=Mz^*+q\). Assume strict complementarity: \(z_i^*+w_i^*>0\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Set \(\alpha=\{i:z_i^*>0\}\). If the principal submatrix \(M_{\alpha\alpha}\) is nonsingular, then there is a neighborhood \(U\) of \(z^*\) such that \(\operatorname{SOL}(M,q)\cap U=\{z^*\}\). Thus \(z^*\) is locally unique, although other solutions may exist outside \(U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly complementary LCP solution is locally unique when the principal submatrix associated with its positive variables is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a neighborhood \(U\) of \(z^*\) such that \(\operatorname{SOL}(M,q)\cap U=\{z^*\}\).

children.title: LCP Degree
children.top_down_role: Degree-based organization of LCP solution structure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The LCP degree on \(\Omega\) is \(\deg(\Phi_{M,q},\Omega,0)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the componentwise minimum-map convention for Brouwer degree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) and \(q\in\mathbb{R}^n\), define the continuous piecewise-linear residual \(\Phi_{M,q}:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) by \(\Phi_{M,q}(z)=\min\{z,Mz+q\}\), with the minimum taken componentwise. Its zeros are exactly the solutions of \(\operatorname{LCP}(M,q)\). If \(\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is bounded and open and \(0\notin\Phi_{M,q}(\partial\Omega)\), the LCP degree in \(\Omega\) is the Brouwer degree \(\deg(\Phi_{M,q},\Omega,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The LCP degree is the Brouwer degree at zero of the componentwise minimum residual, on a region whose boundary contains no solution.
knowledge_statements.title: LCP Degree

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The minimum-map Brouwer-degree definition is coherent and fits the leaf, but LCP degree conventions can differ and no source or locator is supplied to certify this convention.

children.title: LCP Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Behavior of LCP solutions under problem perturbations.

assumptions_latex: The complementarity generalized equation is strongly regular at \(z^*\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The localized solution map \(q\mapsto z(q)\) is single-valued and Lipschitz near \(q^*\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S(q)=\operatorname{SOL}(M,q)\), and suppose \(z^*\in S(q^*)\). If the generalized equation \(0\in Mz+q+N_{\mathbb{R}_+^n}(z)\) is strongly regular at \((z^*,q^*)\), then there exist neighborhoods \(Q\) of \(q^*\) and \(U\) of \(z^*\) such that \(S(q)\cap U=\{z(q)\}\) for every \(q\in Q\). Moreover, some \(L<\infty\) satisfies \(\|z(q_1)-z(q_2)\|\leq L\|q_1-q_2\|\) for all \(q_1,q_2\in Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong regularity makes the nearby LCP solution unique and Lipschitz continuous with respect to perturbations of the right-hand side.

children.title: Degree-Based Stability Regimes
children.top_down_role: Connections between degree structure and sensitivity behavior.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\deg(H(t,\cdot),\Omega,0)\) is constant; a nonzero value guarantees an interior solution throughout the perturbation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States persistence under boundary-safe LCP residual homotopies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be bounded and open, and let \(H:[0,1]\times\overline\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^n\) continuously deform one LCP residual map into another. If \(0\notin H(t,\partial\Omega)\) for every \(t\in[0,1]\), then homotopy invariance gives \(\deg(H(t,\cdot),\Omega,0)=\deg(H(0,\cdot),\Omega,0)\) for every \(t\). If this common degree is nonzero, each perturbed residual has at least one zero in \(\Omega\). This regime ensures existence stability, not uniqueness or Lipschitz sensitivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero LCP degree persists under perturbations that keep the boundary solution-free and guarantees an interior solution, but not uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.title: Degree-Based Stability Regimes

Compute its basic solution. If all basic variables are nonnegative, output \(z\). children.title: Lemke Methods
children.top_down_role: LCP algorithms based on Lemke-style complementary pivoting.

assumptions_latex: A noncycling pivot rule is fixed
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Removal of the artificial variable yields an LCP solution; a secondary ray is a failure certificate for that run.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the classical covering-vector Lemke path procedure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(M\), \(q\), and \(d\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\), augment the system to \(w=Mz+q+dz_0\) with \(z\geq0\), \(w\geq0\), and \(z_0\geq0\). Start from \(z=0\) and the least \(z_0\) making \(w\geq0\), then pivot along almost-complementary bases, using the complement of the leaving variable as the next entering variable. If \(z_0\) leaves the basis, output the resulting \(z\), which solves \(\operatorname{LCP}(M,q)\). If the path reaches a secondary ray, terminate with that ray certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lemke's method follows an augmented almost-complementary path; eliminating the artificial variable gives a solution, while a secondary ray signals failure.
knowledge_statements.title: Lemke Methods

children.title: Pivoting-Framework Comparison
children.top_down_role: Structural distinctions between the two pivoting frameworks.

assumptions_latex: The same finite-dimensional LCP \((M,q)\) is considered
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Principal pivoting searches complementary bases directly, whereas Lemke follows an augmented path; neither framework is universally finite without matrix-class assumptions.

notation.meaning: artificial variable used by Lemke's augmentation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares pivot state spaces and termination outcomes without asserting universal convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Principal pivoting methods operate directly on complementary bases of \(w-Mz=q\) and may require admissibility, finiteness, or matrix-class hypotheses to guarantee success. Lemke methods instead introduce \(z_0\) and \(d\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\), then trace an almost-complementary path in the augmented system. Their successful terminal events differ: principal pivoting reaches a feasible complementary basis, whereas Lemke removes \(z_0\). Their failure modes also differ, including unavailable pivots or cycling for general principal schemes and secondary rays for Lemke. Neither framework is universally finite for arbitrary \(M\) without additional assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Principal methods pivot directly among complementary bases; Lemke follows an augmented path. Their success and failure events differ, and neither is universally finite for arbitrary matrices.
knowledge_statements.title: Pivoting-Framework Comparison

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The comparison fits the exact leaf and carefully avoids universal convergence, but the family-wide termination and failure-mode comparison has no cited source or inspectable locator.

children.title: LCP Splitting Methods
children.top_down_role: Splitting-based algorithms for linear complementarity problems.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any fixed point satisfies \(z=[z-\tau(Mz+q)]_+\), hence solves \(0\le z\perp Mz+q\ge0\).

notation.meaning: componentwise projection onto the nonnegative orthant

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected fixed-point splitting for a finite-dimensional LCP; no convergence rate is asserted.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 11. Interior and Smoothing Methods p. 989
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(z^0\in\mathbb{R}_+^n\), generate \[z^{k+1}=\bigl[z^k-\tau_k(Mz^k+q)\bigr]_+.\] Stop when \(\|z^{k+1}-z^k\|\le\varepsilon\), and return \(z^{k+1}\). For any \(\tau>0\), a vector \(z\) is a fixed point of this update exactly when \(z\ge0\), \(Mz+q\ge0\), and \(z^{\mathsf T}(Mz+q)=0\). Convergence requires additional conditions on \(M\) and the step sizes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Iterate a projected residual step. Every fixed point solves the LCP, although convergence of the iteration requires additional matrix and step-size conditions.
knowledge_statements.title: LCP Splitting Methods

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 11. Interior and Smoothing Methods p. 989
source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-point characterization is mathematically standard, but the cited Chapter 11 locator concerns interior and smoothing methods and does not adequately support this projected splitting iteration or its step rule.

children.title: LCP Regularization Methods
children.top_down_role: Regularization-based algorithms for linear complementarity problems.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every convergent subsequence whose regularized residuals vanish has an LCP solution as its limit.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagonal regularization of an LCP, stated with a residual-based limiting convention.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 11. Interior and Smoothing Methods p. 989
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(k\), approximately solve the regularized problem \[z^k\ge0,\qquad w^k=(M+\varepsilon_k I)z^k+q\ge0,\qquad (z^k)^{\mathsf T}w^k\le\eta_k,\] where \(\eta_k\downarrow0\). Stop when the unregularized complementarity residual meets a prescribed tolerance. If \(z^{k_j}\to\bar z\), then continuity and \(\varepsilon_{k_j}\to0\) imply \(\bar z\ge0\), \(M\bar z+q\ge0\), and \(\bar z^{\mathsf T}(M\bar z+q)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve successively less regularized LCPs. Any convergent subsequence with vanishing errors approaches a solution of the original LCP.
knowledge_statements.title: LCP Regularization Methods

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 11. Interior and Smoothing Methods p. 989
source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The limiting argument is plausible for a convergent subsequence, but the cited locator does not specifically substantiate this diagonal regularization scheme, and its path disagrees with the source inventory. A source specifically supporting regularized LCPs and their limiting conditions is required.

children.title: LCP Newton Methods
children.top_down_role: Newton-type algorithms for linear complementarity problems.

knowledge_statements.title: LCP Newton Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semismooth Newton iteration applied to the Fischer–Burmeister reformulation of a finite-dimensional LCP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\phi(a,b)=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}-a-b\) and \(\Phi_i(z)=\phi(z_i,(Mz+q)_i)\). From \(z^0\in\mathbb{R}^n\), choose \(V_k\in\partial_C\Phi(z^k)\), solve \[V_kd^k=-\Phi(z^k),\] select \(\alpha_k\in(0,1]\) by a merit-function globalization rule, and set \(z^{k+1}=z^k+\alpha_kd^k\). Stop when \(\|\Phi(z^k)\|\le\varepsilon\). A zero of \(\Phi\) satisfies exactly \(0\le z\perp Mz+q\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Apply a generalized Newton step to the Fischer–Burmeister residual, with merit-function globalization. A zero of that residual is exactly an LCP solution.
assumptions_latex: \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), \(q\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(\varepsilon>0\), and each selected Newton matrix \(V_k\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi(z)=0\) holds exactly when \(0\le z\perp Mz+q\ge0\).

children.title: LCP Interior Methods
children.top_down_role: Interior algorithms for linear complementarity problems.

knowledge_statements.title: LCP Interior Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-dual central-path iteration for a finite-dimensional LCP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration \(k\), linearize \[w-Mz-q=0,\qquad z\circ w=\mu_k e\] at a strictly positive pair \((z^k,w^k)\), solve the resulting Newton system for \((\Delta z^k,\Delta w^k)\), and choose a damped step preserving strict positivity and the prescribed central-path neighborhood. Reduce \(\mu_k>0\), stop when the feasibility and complementarity residuals are at most \(\varepsilon\), and return the current pair. If \(\mu_k\to0\), the feasibility residuals and \(z^k\circ w^k\) converge to zero, and \((z^{k_j},w^{k_j})\to(\bar z,\bar w)\), then \(\bar w=M\bar z+q\), \(\bar z\ge0\), \(\bar w\ge0\), and \(\bar z\circ\bar w=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Follow the positive central path by damped Newton steps while reducing the barrier parameter. Every accumulation point obtained with vanishing feasibility and complementarity residuals solves the LCP.
assumptions_latex: \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), \(q\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(\varepsilon>0\), and an initial pair satisfies \(z^0>0\) and \(w^0=Mz^0+q>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\mu_k\to0\) and the feasibility and complementarity residuals vanish, every accumulation point is an LCP solution.

children.title: Pivot Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Failure behavior caused by degenerate pivot configurations.

assumptions_latex: A complementary pivoting tableau represents \(w-Mz=q\) with complementary pairs \((z_i,w_i)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A zero basic variable makes the complementary basic solution degenerate and may destroy uniqueness of the next pivot.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degeneracy in a complementary pivoting tableau, including its algorithmic consequence.

source_refs.locator: 4.3 General Principal Pivoting Methods p. 251
source_refs.source_title: The Linear Complementarity Problem

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A complementary basic feasible solution is pivot-degenerate when at least one basic variable equals \(0\). Then a minimum-ratio test can have ratio \(0\) or multiple attaining rows, so a pivot may change the basis without changing the represented point. Consequently, without an anti-cycling or lexicographic rule, the pivot sequence need not be uniquely determined and may revisit bases even though every tableau remains feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero basic variable creates pivot degeneracy: basis changes can leave the point unchanged, ratio tests can tie, and an unspecified rule can cycle.
knowledge_statements.title: Pivot Degeneracy

children.title: Secondary-Ray Failures
children.top_down_role: Failure behavior associated with secondary rays in complementary pivoting.

knowledge_statements.title: Secondary-Ray Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbounded-path failure of Lemke's complementary pivoting method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In Lemke's augmented system \[w=Mz+q+z_0d,\qquad z\ge0,\quad w\ge0,\quad z_0\ge0,\qquad z_iw_i=0\ \text{for }i=1,\ldots,n,\] a secondary ray is an unbounded edge of the complementary feasible set reached before the artificial variable has been eliminated. If the pivot path enters such a ray, no leaving variable exists for the prescribed entering variable. The method then terminates on the ray rather than at a point with \(z_0=0\), and therefore returns no solution of the original LCP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lemke's method fails on a secondary ray when its augmented complementary path becomes unbounded before the artificial variable is removed.
assumptions_latex: Lemke's augmented system uses a covering vector \(d\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\) and an artificial variable \(z_0\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Entering a secondary ray terminates the pivot search without producing a solution of the original LCP.

children.title: Pivoting Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural regimes separating successful termination from pivoting failure.

assumptions_latex: The task is to solve \(0\le z\perp Mz+q\ge0\) by complementary pivoting.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Outside structural classes guaranteeing solvability and finite termination, a pivot path may degenerate, cycle, or end on a secondary ray.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural boundary of unconditional success for complementary pivoting algorithms.

source_refs.locator: 4.3 General Principal Pivoting Methods p. 251
source_refs.source_title: The Linear Complementarity Problem

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Complementary pivoting has no unconditional finite-solution guarantee for arbitrary \((M,q)\). Degenerate basic solutions can make pivot choices nonunique or permit cycling, and an augmented Lemke path can terminate on a secondary ray. Solvability itself is also necessary: for \(n=1\), \(M=0\), and \(q=-1\), the constraint \(Mz+q\ge0\) is impossible, so no pivoting method can terminate with an LCP solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: General LCP pivoting can fail through degeneracy, cycling, a secondary ray, or simple infeasibility; finite successful termination needs additional structure and pivot rules.
knowledge_statements.title: Pivoting Failure Boundaries

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(a,b)=0\iff a\ge0,\ b\ge0,\ ab=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar Fischer–Burmeister function and its componentwise NCP residual.

source_refs.locator: 7.5 Semismooth Newton Methods p. 692
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Fischer–Burmeister function is \[\phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(a,b)=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}-a-b.\] It represents scalar complementarity exactly: \[\phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(a,b)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
a\ge0,
\ b\ge0,
\ ab=0.\] Hence, for \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\), the componentwise residual \(\Phi_i(x)=\phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(x_i,F_i(x))\) satisfies \(\Phi(x)=0\) exactly when \(0\le x\perp F(x)\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Fischer–Burmeister function vanishes exactly on nonnegative complementary scalar pairs; applying it componentwise converts an NCP into equations.
knowledge_statements.title: Fischer–Burmeister Function Family

source_witnesses.locator: 7.5 Semismooth Newton Methods p. 692
source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

children.title: Minimum Complementarity Function
children.top_down_role: NCP reformulations based on the minimum-map representation.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(\min\{a,b\}=0\iff a\ge0,
\ b\ge0,
\ ab=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar minimum function under the nonnegative complementarity convention.

source_refs.locator: 7.2 Basic Newton-type Methods p. 638
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the minimum complementarity function by \[\phi_{\min}(a,b)=\min\{a,b\}.\] Its zero set is precisely the scalar complementarity set: \[\phi_{\min}(a,b)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
a\ge0,
\ b\ge0,
\ ab=0.\] Thus the nonsmooth equation \(\phi_{\min}(a,b)=0\) simultaneously enforces both nonnegativity conditions and the orthogonality condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimum of two scalars is zero exactly when both are nonnegative and at least one is zero, so it encodes complementarity.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimum Complementarity Function

source_witnesses.locator: 7.2 Basic Newton-type Methods p. 638
source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

children.title: General Complementarity Functions
children.top_down_role: NCP reformulations based on broader complementarity-function families.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The defining equivalence makes componentwise zeros of \(\phi(x_i,F_i(x))\) identical to NCP solutions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of an NCP-function under the nonnegative complementarity convention.

source_refs.locator: 7.2 Basic Newton-type Methods p. 638
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A function \(\phi:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\) is a complementarity function, or NCP-function, when \[\phi(a,b)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
a\ge0,
\ b\ge0,
\ ab=0\] for every \((a,b)\in\mathbb{R}^2\). Given \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\), define \(\Phi_i(x)=\phi(x_i,F_i(x))\). Then \(\Phi(x)=0\) holds exactly when \(x\ge0\), \(F(x)\ge0\), and \(x_iF_i(x)=0\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complementarity function has zeros exactly at nonnegative complementary pairs, so its componentwise residual converts any NCP into a system of equations.
knowledge_statements.title: General Complementarity Functions

source_witnesses.locator: 7.2 Basic Newton-type Methods p. 638
source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

children.title: Minimum-Function Embedding
children.top_down_role: Placement of the minimum function within the general function family.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H(x)=0\iff 0\le x\perp F(x)\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise minimum-function equation representing a finite-dimensional NCP.

source_refs.locator: 7.2 Basic Newton-type Methods p. 638
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(H:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) componentwise by \[H_i(x)=\min\{x_i,F_i(x)\},
\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.\] Then \[H(x)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x\ge0,
\ F(x)\ge0,
\ x_iF_i(x)=0
\ \text{for every }i.\] Thus the nonlinear complementarity problem is represented exactly by the generally nonsmooth equation \(H(x)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Taking the componentwise minimum of the variable and mapping embeds the NCP exactly as a nonsmooth system of equations.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Function Embedding

source_witnesses.locator: 7.2 Basic Newton-type Methods p. 638
source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(\phi_\mu(a,b)=0\iff a>0,
\ b>0,
\ ab=\mu\), and \(\phi_\mu\to\phi_{\mathrm{FB}}\) pointwise as \(\mu\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard positive-parameter smoothing of the Fischer–Burmeister complementarity function.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 11. Interior and Smoothing Methods p. 989
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\mu>0\), define \[\phi_\mu(a,b)=\sqrt{a^2+b^2+2\mu}-a-b.\] This function is continuously differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}^2\), and \[\phi_\mu(a,b)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
a>0,
\ b>0,
\ ab=\mu.\] Moreover, \(\phi_\mu(a,b)\to\sqrt{a^2+b^2}-a-b\) as \(\mu\downarrow0\). Componentwise equations \(\phi_\mu(x_i,F_i(x))=0\) therefore trace a positive perturbed-complementarity system approaching the NCP equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The smoothed Fischer–Burmeister function is smooth for positive parameter, represents positive perturbed complementarity, and converges to the original complementarity function.
knowledge_statements.title: Smoothed NCP Functions

children.title: Pointwise Fischer–Burmeister Regularity
children.top_down_role: Fischer–Burmeister regularity assessed at individual points.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\) is pointwise FB-regular precisely when every matrix in \(\partial_B\Phi(\bar x)\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the generalized-Jacobian nonsingularity formulation of pointwise FB regularity.

source_refs.locator: 9.1.2 Pointwise FB regularity p. 809
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\), define \(\Phi_i(x)=\sqrt{x_i^2+F_i(x)^2}-x_i-F_i(x)\). A solution \(\bar x\) of \(\Phi(x)=0\) is pointwise Fischer–Burmeister regular if
\[
\det V\ne0\qquad\text{for every }V\in\partial_B\Phi(\bar x).
\]
Equivalently, because \(\partial_B\Phi(\bar x)\) is compact, there exists \(\kappa<\infty\) such that \(\|V^{-1}\|\le\kappa\) for every \(V\in\partial_B\Phi(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the solution, every limiting Jacobian of the Fischer–Burmeister residual is nonsingular, equivalently their inverses are uniformly bounded.
knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise Fischer–Burmeister Regularity

source_witnesses.locator: 9.1.2 Pointwise FB regularity p. 809
source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated condition is standard BD-regularity of the Fischer–Burmeister residual, but it cannot be identified with the source's exact notion of pointwise FB regularity without inspecting the cited section.

children.title: Sequential Fischer–Burmeister Regularity
children.top_down_role: Fischer–Burmeister regularity assessed along convergent sequences.

assumptions_latex: \(\Phi(\bar x)=0\), where \(\Phi\) is the Fischer–Burmeister residual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Sequential FB regularity requires uniform invertibility along every convergent sequence of residual Jacobians.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential formulation based on uniformly bounded inverses of nearby limiting Jacobians.

source_refs.locator: 9.1.3 Sequential FB regularity p. 816
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The solution \(\bar x\) is sequentially Fischer–Burmeister regular if, for every sequence \(x^k\to\bar x\) at differentiability points of \(\Phi\), the matrices \(V_k=\nabla\Phi(x^k)\) are nonsingular for all sufficiently large \(k\) and
\[
\sup_{k\ge k_0}\|V_k^{-1}\|<\infty.
\]
Equivalently, the same requirement may be imposed on arbitrary selections \(V_k\in\partial_B\Phi(x^k)\) with \(x^k\to\bar x\), provided the generalized Jacobian convention is fixed accordingly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All limiting Jacobians along every sequence approaching the solution eventually remain nonsingular with uniformly bounded inverses.
knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Fischer–Burmeister Regularity

source_witnesses.locator: 9.1.3 Sequential FB regularity p. 816
source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The differentiability-point formulation and the arbitrary Bouligand-selection formulation are asserted to be equivalent without the hypotheses needed to establish that equivalence. The cited definition must be inspected before selecting the correct version.

children.title: Pointwise-to-Sequential Regularity Relations
children.top_down_role: Implication and separation regimes connecting the two regularity notions.

assumptions_latex: \(\partial_B\Phi\) is nonempty, locally bounded, compact-valued, and outer semicontinuous at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist \(r>0\) and \(\kappa<\infty\) such that \(\|V^{-1}\|\le\kappa\) whenever \(\|x-\bar x\|<r\) and \(V\in\partial_B\Phi(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates pointwise and sequential notions under compactness and outer semicontinuity.

source_refs.locator: 9.1.2 Pointwise FB regularity p. 809; 9.1.3 Sequential FB regularity p. 816
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\partial_B\Phi\) be nonempty, locally bounded, compact-valued, and outer semicontinuous at \(\bar x\). If every \(V\in\partial_B\Phi(\bar x)\) is nonsingular, then there exist \(r>0\) and \(\kappa<\infty\) such that
\[
\|V^{-1}\|\le\kappa
\quad\text{whenever}\quad
\|x-\bar x\|<r,\;V\in\partial_B\Phi(x).
\]
Consequently, pointwise FB regularity implies sequential FB regularity. Conversely, sequential regularity applied to the constant sequence \(x^k=\bar x\) implies pointwise regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under compactness and outer semicontinuity, pointwise FB regularity yields uniform nearby nonsingularity and hence sequential regularity; the converse follows from constant sequences.
knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise-to-Sequential Regularity Relations

source_witnesses.locator: 9.1.2 Pointwise FB regularity p. 809; 9.1.3 Sequential FB regularity p. 816
source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

children.title: Newton Nonsingularity
children.top_down_role: NCP regimes with nonsingular Newton linearizations.

assumptions_latex: \(\Phi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is locally Lipschitz near a zero \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Newton nonsingularity holds when every admissible generalized Jacobian at \(\bar x\) is invertible.

notation.meaning: chosen generalized Jacobian used by the Newton method

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semismooth Newton nonsingularity for an NCP residual equation.

source_refs.locator: 7.5 Semismooth Newton Methods p. 692
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a locally Lipschitz NCP residual \(\Phi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) and a generalized Jacobian model \(\mathcal J\Phi(x)\), Newton nonsingularity at a solution \(\bar x\) means
\[
\det V\ne0\qquad\text{for all }V\in\mathcal J\Phi(\bar x).
\]
A uniform local version requires numbers \(r>0\) and \(\kappa<\infty\) satisfying \(\|V^{-1}\|\le\kappa\) for every \(V\in\mathcal J\Phi(x)\) whenever \(\|x-\bar x\|<r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every generalized Jacobian admissible in the Newton model is invertible at the solution; the uniform version bounds all nearby inverses.
knowledge_statements.title: Newton Nonsingularity

children.title: Level-Set Boundedness
children.top_down_role: NCP regimes with bounded merit-function level sets.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Level-set boundedness is the boundedness of \(\{x:\Psi(x)\le\Psi(x^0)\}\).

notation.meaning: merit function, commonly half the squared NCP residual norm

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundedness condition for the initial merit-function level set.

source_refs.locator: 9.1.5 Boundedness of level sets p. 826
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonnegative NCP merit function \(\Psi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) and initial point \(x^0\), define
\[
L_0=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\Psi(x)\le\Psi(x^0)\}.
\]
The level-set boundedness condition holds at \(x^0\) when \(L_0\) is bounded. If \(\Psi\) is continuous, this condition makes \(L_0\) compact. For the residual merit function, one takes \(\Psi(x)=\tfrac12\|\Phi(x)\|^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The set of points whose merit value does not exceed the initial value is bounded, and is compact when the merit function is continuous.

children.title: Regularity–Boundedness Interaction
children.top_down_role: Structural connections between Newton regularity and level-set control.

knowledge_statements.title: Regularity–Boundedness Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative coupling of merit-level confinement and uniformly nonsingular Newton models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Phi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(\Psi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be a merit function, and fix \(x^0\in\mathbb{R}^n\). Define
\[
L_0=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\Psi(x)\le\Psi(x^0)\}.
\]
Suppose \(L_0\) is compact and \(\mathcal J\Phi(x)\) is a nonempty family of \(n\times n\) matrices such that
\[
\|V^{-1}\|\le\kappa<\infty
\quad\text{for every }x\in L_0\text{ and }V\in\mathcal J\Phi(x).
\]
Then, for every admissible pair \((x,V)\), the Newton equation
\[
Vd=-\Phi(x)
\]
has a unique solution satisfying \(\|d\|\le\kappa\|\Phi(x)\|\). Moreover, every sequence \((x^k)\) with \(x^0\) as its initial point and \(\Psi(x^{k+1})\le\Psi(x^k)\) remains in \(L_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform invertibility on the compact initial merit level set uniquely defines each Newton step and bounds it by the residual. Any merit-nonincreasing iteration remains in that level set.
assumptions_latex: \(\Phi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\Psi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) are given, with initial point \(x^0\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
\(\mathcal J\Phi(x)\) is nonempty and \(\|V^{-1}\|\le\kappa<\infty\) for every \(x\in L_0\) and \(V\in\mathcal J\Phi(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every equation \(Vd=-\Phi(x)\) with \(x\in L_0\) and \(V\in\mathcal J\Phi(x)\) has a unique solution satisfying \(\|d\|\le\kappa\|\Phi(x)\|\), and every merit-nonincreasing iteration remains in \(L_0\).

children.title: Fischer–Burmeister Algorithms
children.top_down_role: NCP equation algorithms using Fischer–Burmeister reformulations.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iteration applies a semismooth Newton step to \(\Phi(x)=0\) and globalizes it through the merit function \(\Psi(x)=\tfrac12\|\Phi(x)\|^2\).

source_refs.locator: 7.5 Semismooth Newton Methods p. 692
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x^0\), tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), and \(\Psi(x)=\tfrac12\|\Phi(x)\|^2\), repeat while \(\|\Phi(x^k)\|>\varepsilon\): choose \(V_k\in\partial_B\Phi(x^k)\), solve
\[
V_kd^k=-\Phi(x^k),
\]
and choose \(\alpha_k\in(0,1]\) by backtracking until \(\Psi(x^k+\alpha_kd^k)\) satisfies a prescribed sufficient-decrease test. Set \(x^{k+1}=x^k+\alpha_kd^k\). Output the first iterate satisfying \(\|\Phi(x^k)\|\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve generalized Newton systems for the Fischer–Burmeister residual, globalize by merit-function backtracking, and stop when the residual meets tolerance.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x^0\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), define \(M_i(x)=\min\{x_i,F_i(x)\}\). children.title: NCP-Map Algorithm Comparison
children.top_down_role: Structural comparison of algorithms induced by the two NCP maps.

knowledge_statements.title: NCP-Map Algorithm Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares solution equivalence and local structure of the minimum and Fischer–Burmeister NCP maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuously differentiable, and define
\[
M_i(x)=\min\{x_i,F_i(x)\},
\qquad
\Phi_i(x)=\sqrt{x_i^2+F_i(x)^2}-x_i-F_i(x).
\]
For every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
M(x)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\Phi(x)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x\ge0,\;F(x)\ge0,\;x^{\mathsf T}F(x)=0.
\]
Thus algorithms based on the two maps target the same NCP solution set. The minimum map directly exposes branch-dependent active sets, whereas the Fischer–Burmeister map is symmetric in each complementary pair and is smooth wherever \((x_i,F_i(x))\ne(0,0)\) for every \(i\). Their generalized Newton matrices and globalization behavior need not coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimum and Fischer–Burmeister maps have exactly the same zeros as the nonlinear complementarity problem, although their local generalized derivatives, active-set structures, and resulting algorithms can differ.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the conditions \(M(x)=0\), \(\Phi(x)=0\), and \(x\ge0,\;F(x)\ge0,\;x^{\mathsf T}F(x)=0\) are equivalent.

children.top_down_role: NCP methods globalized through trust-region mechanisms.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each step approximately minimizes \(m_k\) over \(\|d\|\le\Delta_k\), and the actual-to-predicted reduction ratio controls acceptance and radius updates.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x^0\), \(\Delta_0>0\), and \(\Psi(x)=\tfrac12\|\Phi(x)\|^2\), choose \(V_k\in\partial_B\Phi(x^k)\) and approximately solve
\[
\min_{\|d\|\le\Delta_k}m_k(d),
\qquad m_k(d)=\tfrac12\|\Phi(x^k)+V_kd\|^2.
\]
Compute \(\rho_k=[\Psi(x^k)-\Psi(x^k+d^k)]/[m_k(0)-m_k(d^k)]\). Accept \(x^{k+1}=x^k+d^k\) when \(\rho_k\) exceeds a prescribed threshold; otherwise set \(x^{k+1}=x^k\). Update \(\Delta_k\) according to \(\rho_k\), and stop at the specified residual tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize a linearized residual model inside a radius, then accept the step and update the radius using actual versus predicted reduction.
knowledge_statements.title: Trust-Region NCP Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x^0\in C\), construct at iteration \(k\) a local model \(q_k(d)\) of \(\Psi(x^k+d)\) and compute an approximate solution of
\[
\min_d q_k(d)\qquad\text{subject to}\qquad x^k+d\in C.
\]
Globalize the trial direction by selecting \(\alpha_k\in(0,1]\) such that \(x^k+\alpha_kd^k\in C\) and a prescribed sufficient-decrease test for \(\Psi\) holds. Set \(x^{k+1}=x^k+\alpha_kd^k\), and stop when the residual or an appropriate constrained-stationarity measure is below tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximately minimize a local NCP merit model subject to feasibility, globalize along a feasible segment, and stop at residual or stationarity tolerance.
knowledge_statements.title: Constrained NCP Methods

children.title: Trust-Region Constrained Regimes
children.top_down_role: NCP methods combining constrained formulations with trust-region globalization.

assumptions_latex: \(q_k\) is a local model at a feasible iterate \(x^k\), and \(\Delta_k>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The trial step satisfies both \(x^k+d\in C\) and \(\|d\|\le\Delta_k\); model agreement governs acceptance and radius adjustment.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combined feasibility and trust-region globalization regime.

source_refs.locator: 9.1.7 A trust region approach p. 839; 9.1.8 Constrained methods p. 844
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At a feasible iterate \(x^k\in C\), the trust-region constrained regime computes a trial step from
\[
\min_d q_k(d)
\qquad\text{subject to}
\qquad x^k+d\in C,
\quad \|d\|\le\Delta_k.
\]
The feasibility constraint encodes the admissible NCP reformulation, while the radius limits reliance on the local model. A trial step is accepted only when its actual merit reduction is adequate relative to its predicted reduction; this ratio also determines contraction, retention, or enlargement of \(\Delta_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The step must be both feasible and inside the trust region; actual-versus-predicted merit reduction controls acceptance and radius changes.
knowledge_statements.title: Trust-Region Constrained Regimes

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the generalized box \([l,u]\), the inclusion \(0\in F(x)+N_{[l,u]}(x)\) gives every coordinate regime. Two finite endpoints give bounded-variable complementarity; replacing \(u_i\) by \(+\infty\) removes the upper-bound case; replacing \(l_i\) by \(-\infty\) removes the lower-bound case; and \((l_i,u_i)=(-\infty,+\infty)\) forces \(F_i(x)=0\). Thus changing an endpoint between a finite value and infinity effects the corresponding bound-regime transition without changing the normal-cone formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extended-real bounds unify bounded, one-sided, and free variables; moving an endpoint to infinity deletes its associated boundary condition.

children.title: Differentiability–Monotonicity Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Interaction between smoothness structure and monotone geometry in implicit MCPs.

assumptions_latex: \(U\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is open and convex, and \(G:U\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is continuously differentiable.
\(G(x)=F(x,s(x))\), where the differentiable implicit map \(s\) satisfies the nonsingularity assumptions of the implicit-function theorem.

notation.meaning: Symmetric part of the reduced Jacobian.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The differentiable reduced map \(G\) is monotone on \(U\) if and only if \[\operatorname{sym}DG(x):=\tfrac12\bigl(DG(x)+DG(x)^{\mathsf T}\bigr)\succeq0\qquad\text{for every }x\in U.\] When \(s\) is defined by \(H(x,s(x))=0\), the Jacobian tested here is \[DG=D_xF-D_yF(D_yH)^{-1}D_xH,\] with all derivatives evaluated at \((x,s(x))\). knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two scalar examples isolate loss of smoothness and loss of monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Loss of smoothness occurs even for smooth implicit data: let \(H(x,y)=y^3-x\) and \(F(x,y)=y\). The unique solution is \(s(x)=\sqrt[3]{x}\), so \(G(x)=\sqrt[3]{x}\) is not differentiable at \(0\); here \(D_yH(0,0)=0\). Loss of monotonicity can occur without loss of smoothness: let \(H(x,y)=y-x\) and \(F(x,y)=-y\). Then \(s(x)=x\) and \(G(x)=-x\), for which \((G(x)-G(z))(x-z)=-(x-z)^2<0\) whenever \(x\ne z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singular implicit equation can destroy differentiability, while a smooth implicit substitution can produce an antimonotone reduced residual.
knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Smooth or Monotone Structure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Implicit MCP whose auxiliary map is generated by a parametric KKT system.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Constrained Optimization and Equilibria p. 3
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each parameter \(x\in C\), let \(s(x)=(y(x),\lambda(x))\) satisfy the lower-level KKT system \[\nabla_yL(x,y,\lambda)=0,\qquad g(x,y)\le0,\qquad \lambda\ge0,\qquad \lambda_jg_j(x,y)=0\ \text{for every }j.\] Given an outer residual \(F(x,y,\lambda)\), define \(G(x)=F(x,s(x))\). The KKT-map implicit MCP is to find \(x\in C\) satisfying \(0\in G(x)+N_C(x)\), equivalently the coordinate complementarity conditions determined by the bounds of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve a parametric KKT system, substitute its selected primal-dual solution into the outer residual, and impose the resulting box MCP.
knowledge_statements.title: KKT-Map Implicit MCPs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed construction fits the topic in broad terms, but the cited chapter-level opening page does not specifically support this KKT-map implicit MCP definition. The dimensions and domains of g, lambda, F, and the index j are not introduced, and the conditions under which a single-valued KKT selection exists are left entirely external to the statement. A more specific source and a fully typed formulation are needed.
